works.title: Self-Evolving Embodied Agents via Skill-Harness Evolution

publication.actor: Frozen Qwen3.6-27B planner; VLABench π0 executor or ESI-Bench interaction API
publication.summary: Evolves reusable skills and context-handling code around a frozen embodied planner and executor.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Optimizes skills first, then the harness, using beam search and disjoint training, validation and evaluation episodes. VLABench evaluation includes 800 held-out episodes across four custom splits: C1 is in-domain, while C2–C4 shift the target category, the task form, or both.
Results and comparison
VLABench success is 28.25% for the seed, 33.50% for skill-only, 30.50% for harness-only and 34.50% for the combined system. On 231 ESI-Bench questions, micro accuracy rises from 32.5% to 49.8%.
Evaluation context

The component results compare complete configurations; effects are not additive. The published GPT-5 reference uses another evaluation scope and is not a paired baseline. These are benchmark environments rather than a physical deployment study.

works.title: AI as a Compiler: Compiling Triton Kernels Without the Triton Compiler

publication.scope: LLM lowering of Triton to PTX
publication.actor: GPT-6 Astra is the compiler LLM (TAIC) and its subagents write alternative patches; GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 variants are compared only on FP16 GEMM. No model is trained.
publication.summary: An LLM agent lowers fixed Triton kernels directly to PTX, keeping only candidates that assemble, pass differential tests and run faster.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each task fixes a compilation contract: Triton source, compile-time constants, launch grid, argument ABI and target GPU. TAIC writes PTX; TCEnv assembles and sanitizes it (memory safety and race freedom are required), runs randomized differential tests against the Triton reference with inputs that stress overflow, underflow and cancellation, then times it and returns selected Nsight Compute metrics. TAIC diagnoses a bottleneck, subagents implement alternative patches, and only safe, correct and faster candidates seed the next round until the API budget is spent. Humans supply the contract, hand-improved and autotuned Triton baselines, tolerances and three skills (NCU interpretation, PTX ISA lookup, optimization principles).
Results and comparison

Against autotuned Triton 3.6.0 on L40S, H100 and B200, twelve common kernels range from 0.83× (FP16 GEMM, H100) to 2.23× (convolution), with elementwise kernels within about 1% of Triton. On ten kernels from recent papers (B200, $15 budget) it reports 3.34× on BitDelta, 1.55× on FlashSinkhorn, 1.41× on SageAttention and 1.37× on FlashAttention; Lion, Dion and Mamba-2 stay near parity. Five repeated B200 runs give 2.004 ± 0.197× on FP8 convolution and 1.236 ± 0.106× on FlashAttention. On FP16 GEMM, the GPT-5.x models reach 0.73×–0.97× or no accepted kernel.
Evaluation context

Correctness is empirical, and the paper gives neither the number of test inputs nor tolerance values. When the original Volta equivalence checker gates acceptance, B200 FP16 results fall to 0.24× (GEMM), 0.78× (FlashAttention) and 0.77× (convolution). The authors extend Volta to Hopper and Blackwell features (trusted base 42k → 60k lines) without claiming soundness; atomics, input-dependent control flow and bit-level float tricks remain unverifiable. Main-grid results are single runs at fixed problem sizes. Elementwise searches cost under $1.50 and GEMM or convolution about $5–$12 per kernel.

works.title: KernelZero: Co-Evolving Proposer and Coder for Continuously Improved GPU Kernel Generation

publication.actor: Proposer and Coder are separate Qwen2.5-Coder-7B models trained with GRPO while the other is frozen; gpt-oss-120B supplies cold-start distillation traces for the Coder.
publication.summary: Alternates GRPO on a module Proposer rewarded for near-50% Coder success and a CUDA/Triton Coder rewarded with correctness-gated speedup.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

The Proposer turns Torch API sets, sampled from a 442-API co-occurrence pool, into runnable modules that must pass AST, execution and NaN/Inf checks; its frontier reward peaks when about half of five Coder samples are correct. The Coder is first distilled on 42,454 CUDA and 59,998 Triton traces that gpt-oss-120B wrote for cudaLLM tasks and that passed correctness checks, then trained with CA-GRPO, where speedup rewards switch on only once a group's correctness rate reaches 0.5. The models alternate for 4 rounds of 20 steps; each 20-step update takes about 3.1 h (Proposer, 12 A100s) or 4.5 h (Coder).
Results and comparison

On KernelBench Levels 1/2 (A100-80GB, one-shot prompts), KernelZero-7B reports CUDA pass@1 of 75.8%/69.6% (pass@10 100%/97%) and Triton pass@1 of 77.2%/72.5%. Claude-4.5-Sonnet reaches 76.4%/66.5% CUDA pass@1, and Dr.Kernel-8B (three turns) reaches 73.0% Triton pass@1 on Level 2. Speed is weaker for CUDA: fast1@1 is 17.6%/2.4% versus 43.9%/65.4% for Triton, all relative to PyTorch eager. Continuing Proposer training after step 40, instead of freezing it, adds 0.9/5.2 CUDA and 2.3/4.2 Triton pass@1 points.
Evaluation context

Correctness copies the reference state_dict and compares outputs with atol = rtol = 1e-2; the number of input trials is not stated. Timing averages three CUDA-event runs after two warm-ups. Generated code may not delegate the computation to PyTorch ops, and the CUDA kernels call no cuBLAS/cuDNN while the eager reference does, so CUDA speedups on GEMM- and convolution-heavy Level 2 tasks face a vendor-library baseline. Level 3, torch.compile baselines and variance across training runs are not reported.

works.title: AMDKernelVault: Large-Scale Datasets and Agentic Training for AMD GPU Kernel Optimization

publication.scope: AMD HIP/Triton kernel corpus and training
publication.actor: GPT-5 generates most HIP data; gpt-oss-120B, DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen2.5-32B generate Triton data; Qwen3-8B is trained with SFT and GRPO and then serves as generator, reflector and optimizer.
publication.summary: Agentic generate–evaluate–reflect pipelines build execution-verified AMD HIP and Triton kernels, which train a Qwen3-8B kernel agent through SFT and execution-rewarded RL.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

HIPKernelGen and TritonKernelGen turn PyTorch references from CUDA-Agent-Ops-6K, GPUMODE KernelBook, the AI CUDA Engineer archive, Stack-v2 and TritonBench-8k into candidates that are compiled under ROCm, checked with torch.allclose (HIP default rtol = atol = 1e-4; Triton fallback rtol 1e-4, atol 1e-3) and latency-profiled, with reflector-guided retries. The release holds 62,153 verified HIP samples, 2,377 rocBLAS/rocSOLVER QA entries and 39,893 Triton kernels. Qwen3-8B then receives SFT, single-turn GRPO for HIP and three-turn GRPO for Triton, rewarded 0.4 for compiling, 1.0 for correctness and a speedup term capped at 1.5.
Results and comparison

On 200 KernelBench L1/L2 PyTorch-to-HIP tasks, correctness pass@1 rises from 14.5% (base) to 34.0% after SFT+RL, versus 24.0% for GPT-5 and 22.0% for Claude Sonnet 4. On 100 held-out HIP-to-HIP tasks it reaches 84% correctness against GPT-5's 87%. In a fixed three-iteration GEAK OptimAgent-v2 loop on MI355X, TritonBench-G Corr@3 is 33.2% (Claude Sonnet 4: 29.8%) and ROCmBench Corr@3 is 41.94% (Claude: 35.48%), though Claude keeps higher ROCmBench Comp@3 and speed (1.82× vs 1.61×). Single-turn RL scores 13.1 points lower on TritonBench-G.
Evaluation context

Speedups are relative to the PyTorch reference for translation and to the input kernel for kernel-to-kernel tasks, using median GPU-event timing with L2 flushes; no torch.compile or rocBLAS comparison is reported. Train/test separation is by source and task identifier only, and the authors did not run a semantic near-duplicate audit. Triton validation discards candidates that pass only input- or shape-specialized checks; no other anti-cheating checks are described. ROCm and PyTorch versions vary across data snapshots, and frontier comparisons use a single agent budget.

works.title: CUDA-Harness: Harnessing Agentic CUDA Kernel Generation and Optimization from Natural Language

publication.actor: Seed2.0 Lite (thinking disabled) runs the ReAct agent in the main results; DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.1 replace it in cross-model tests. No model is trained.
publication.summary: Plans kernels from natural-language prompts, synthesizes isolated test data, and refines CUDA over three rounds, reverting to conservative code whenever validation fails.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

The agent first writes a kernel manifest (inputs, outputs, algorithm, language-agnostic reference code, test shapes and dtypes), then fills a self-contained CUDA scaffold that reads test inputs from files and forbids dummy inputs. Test inputs and reference outputs are produced separately with NumPy or PyTorch and drawn from wide ranges (for example Gaussian mean 5, standard deviation 10) so the absolute tolerance cannot dominate. MCP tools check compilation, then atol/rtol correctness, then Nsight Systems latency. Failed validation triggers a retreat to a simpler kernel; otherwise three rounds of three candidates are guided by diff-and-reward insights kept within the task.
Results and comparison

On CUDABench with an A40 GPU, the full harness reports 99.7% compilation, 80.5% functional correctness and RScore 110.7 (mean of 1/ms, zero for incorrect kernels), versus 90.1%, 60.9% and 80.1 for the official CUDABench procedure; Codex reaches 69.5% correctness and CudaForge 67.7%. The margin is largest on the least-specified Level 3 prompts (70.4% vs 47.6%). Removing correctness-first refinement drops correctness to 70.8%. Synthesized validation agrees with benchmark validation in 84.4% of cases; its 8.7% false positives come from prompt misreadings, skipped post-processing and a CUDABench data-loading defect.
Evaluation context

RScore averages inverse latency, so short-running tasks weigh most, and it is not a speedup over cuBLAS, PyTorch or expert CUDA. The paper gives no task count, tolerance values or number of synthesized inputs. Each kernel is generated once, and variance, tokens and wall-clock cost are not reported. Cross-model, cross-GPU (GTX 1660 SUPER, Jetson AGX Orin) and C-to-CUDA tests (BabelTower: 97.1% vs 90.1% correctness) keep the same ordering; one cross-model correctness value is reported as 101.8%.

works.title: Multi-turn RL with Structural and Performance Aware Rewards for CUDA Kernel Generation

publication.actor: Qwen-3-32B (4-bit QLoRA) is the RL policy and also generates the CUDA variants used to train an MLP ranker that supplies the structural reward; another LLM summarizes earlier turns.
publication.summary: GRPO trains Qwen-3-32B to write CUDA using execution rewards plus a learned ranker's score over static code features such as coalescing and occupancy.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Eleven features (coalescing, arithmetic intensity, occupancy proxy, divergence, transfers, atomics, synchronizations, kernel count, threads per block, global accesses, operations) are extracted statically from CUDA code. An MLP ranker learns pairwise preferences between top- and bottom-quartile candidates by measured speedup, using about 50k generated variants filtered to 2,903 C and 1,013 PyTorch programs. GRPO then samples 16 candidates per program; the reward adds compile and pass-rate penalties, clipped log2 speedup, a runtime-variance penalty and the ranker score. Up to five refinement turns feed back compiler errors, failed tests, speedup and structural notes.
Results and comparison

All headline numbers are pass@5. On KernelBench PyTorch-to-CUDA (250 tasks), CUDAPERF reports 93% correctness and a 6.41× geometric-mean speedup, versus 86% and 3.09× for CUDA Agent (run from its public agent workdir) and 82% and 1.10× for Kevin-32B; its pass@1 is 55% and 1.9×. On C-to-CUDA it reports 89% and 11.02× on its own dataset and 94% and 9.02× on BabelTower, where QiMeng-MuPa also reaches 94% correctness. Removing the structural reward gives 84% and 4.3× on KernelBench; removing the execution reward gives 76% and 3.7×.
Evaluation context

Speedup is defined as sequential-program time over CUDA time (the text gives both median and mean of five runs), and the reference device for KernelBench PyTorch programs is not stated, so these figures are not comparable with eager-GPU or torch.compile speedups. Correctness means passing at least five test cases with no stated tolerance, and no checks for PyTorch fallback or library calls are described. BabelTower feeds the curated training data and is also a test set, with no decontamination reported. Each RL run takes about 3.4–3.5 days on two A100-40GB GPUs.

works.title: Optimizing CUDA like a Human: Micro-Profiling Tools as Expert Surrogates for LLM-Based GPU Kernel Optimization

publication.actor: Claude Sonnet 4.6 generates candidate kernels and profile analyses; a separate background LLM call extracts search memory. No model is trained.
publication.summary: Turns Nsight Compute, Nsight Systems and SASS metrics into rule-based diagnostic advice that guides an MCTS search over complete CUDA kernels.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A benchmarking agent classifies each reference with a roofline estimate, and the class selects which of 15 hand-written micro-profiling tools (8 ncu, 5 nsys, 2 SASS) run on every compiled candidate, each emitting severity, root cause and ranked fixes. A programmer agent proposes two candidates per iteration and can search the CUTLASS/CuTe source tree. MCTS uses progressive widening, rewards ln(speedup) for correct kernels, −2 for wrong output and −3 for crashes, and prunes dead ends. Search memory is scoped to a single run. Correctness uses torch.allclose with atol 1e-2 and rtol 1e-3.
Results and comparison

On KernelBench with A100 GPUs, it reports geometric-mean speedups over PyTorch eager of 2.42×, 4.69× and 5.30× on Levels 1–3 and solves all 250 tasks, versus KernelBlaster's published 1.43×/2.50×/1.50× on H100. On a 42-task subset, full tools reach 4.00× versus 3.35× with no profiling feedback and 1.77× with raw ncu counters; MCTS beats greedy 4.60× to 3.65× (p = 0.004), and search memory's +6% is not significant. On a VeOmni MoE weight-gradient kernel (H100) it reports 1.23× over hand-tuned Triton with a from-scratch CuTe WGMMA kernel.
Evaluation context

Each task runs 15 seeds (5 temperatures × 3 rounds) of 30 iterations with two candidates each, and the tool ablation reports the best speedup across seeds, so figures are best-of-many. The KernelBlaster comparison uses published numbers from a different GPU. Solutions may call cuBLAS/CUTLASS, which is the tensor-core tool's highest-impact advice, and an appendix solution casts FP32 inputs to BF16 under the 1e-2 tolerance. The Level 2 mean falls from 4.69× to 3.25× when per-task speedups are capped at 10×. Search cost and torch.compile baselines are not reported.

works.title: daVinci-kernel: Co-Evolving Skill Selection, Summarization, and Utilization via RL for GPU Kernel Optimization

publication.scope: RL with an evolving skill library
publication.actor: One Qwen3-8B-Base or Qwen3-14B-Base backbone acts as skill selector, multi-turn Triton policy and skill summarizer, all trained jointly; GPT-5.4 trajectories seed the SFT data.
publication.summary: Jointly RL-trains one model to select, apply and write kernel-optimization skills; new skills enter the library only after re-execution confirms speedup.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Following Dr. Kernel's TRLOO objective, the policy writes Triton kernels over multiple turns with reward correctness × (1 + speedup + share of runtime in generated kernels). Each task gets three skill schemes plus a no-skill scheme with four rollouts each; BM25 pre-filters 20 skills and the model reranks up to three. Rollouts whose best turn exceeds both 1.2× and 1.2 times the first-turn speedup trigger two summary calls. A rule filter rejects skills suggesting PyTorch or torch.compile fallbacks, and a skill is kept only if re-running the policy with it meets the same thresholds.
Results and comparison

On KernelBench (Fast_x = share of tasks at least x× faster than the PyTorch reference), daVinci-kernel-14B reports Fast_1 of 37.2%, 70.6% and 32.2% on Levels 1–3, against 30.4%, 58.5% and 22.1% for the authors' reproduction of Dr. Kernel-14B; at Fast_1.2, Level 3 rises from 2.8% to 7.3%. Withholding skills at inference drops 14B Level 3 Fast_1 to 11.5%. Skill-free RL beats the full 8B model at Level 2 Fast_1 (51.6% vs 44.8%) but trails at Fast_2 (2.1% vs 7.9%).
Evaluation context

The reproduced Dr. Kernel scores differ widely from that paper's own figures (14B Level 3 Fast_1: 22.1% vs 8.8%), and frontier-model rows are copied from Dr. Kernel. GPU type, samples per task and seeds are not stated. A case study credits a 2.0× Level 2 result to a skill that skips Conv3D and GroupNorm because the task's min and clamp make every output zero, and retrieved skills advise keeping GEMM and convolution in cuBLAS/cuDNN, so part of the gain comes from task-specific shortcuts and retained vendor kernels. Training takes about 1,734 s per step.

works.title: DRTriton: Large-Scale Synthetic Data Driven Reinforcement Learning for Triton Kernel Generation

publication.actor: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct is SFT- and DRPO-trained into DRTriton-7B; DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-5.2 write SFT kernels; GPT-5.2, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-Coder-480B and AutoTriton are frozen baselines
publication.summary: A 7B model is RL-trained on 100K solver-generated PyTorch programs of rising difficulty, with decoupled correctness and log-speedup rewards and fragment-level test-time search.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

CSP-DAG samples random operator graphs over 61 PyTorch operators and solves tensor-shape constraints with CP-SAT under FLOP and size bounds; difficulty is the operator count. SFT uses 2,026 verified single-operator pairs written by DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-5.2. DRPO then trains on 20K one-operator, 60K two-operator and 20K five-operator programs, advancing when held-out pass@1 exceeds 50%; correct outputs are weighted by a log-speedup reward and incorrect ones penalized, under a KL constraint. Verification requires @triton.jit, a no-op monkey-patch test showing the Triton kernels are used, and exact output match on 5 inputs. Training took about 10 days on 8 H100.
Results and comparison

On 400 held-out synthetic programs, DRTriton reaches 87/75/15% accuracy on 1/2/5-operator programs without search, versus 68/49/7% for Claude-Sonnet-4.5. On KernelBench, lowered to functional form with torch.export and run with test-time search, it reports 69/96/76% accuracy on Levels 1/2/3, with 17/92/54% faster than eager PyTorch and 12/56/34% faster than torch.compile; GPT-5.2 without search reaches 40/32/30% accuracy and 23/23/18% faster than eager. DRPO beats GRPO on the same first-stage data, and a log speed reward beats power-law forms.
Evaluation context

DRTriton's KernelBench numbers rely on test-time search: every contiguous fragment of up to 5 operators is translated, verified and timed, and the fastest hybrid is kept with remaining operators in PyTorch, costing 3.53 h of generation and validation for 250 tasks versus 0.08 h without search. DRTriton without search is not reported on KernelBench, and only AutoTriton receives the same search. In the LeNet-5 walkthrough only the first conv2d+ReLU is fused into Triton. The synthetic operator set was chosen to include KernelBench operators.

works.title: Dr. Kernel: Reinforcement Learning Done Right for Triton Kernel Generations

publication.scope: Multi-turn Triton RL with hacking checks
publication.actor: Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen3-14B-Base are cold-started on GPT-5 trajectories and RL-trained into Dr. Kernel-8B/14B; GPT-5, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, AutoTriton and open models are frozen baselines
publication.summary: Multi-turn RL in a distributed GPU gym trains Qwen3 models to write Triton kernels, with execution-based hacking checks and profiling-weighted rewards against lazy optimization.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

KernelGym is a server–worker evaluator (FastAPI, Redis) that runs each kernel in an isolated subprocess, one task per GPU, and returns correctness, speedup, profiler summaries and a hacking flag. Cold start uses 8K cudaLLM queries with 5-turn GPT-5 trajectories. RL uses cudaLLM queries for 300 rollout steps, 16 rollouts of up to 3 turns, reward = correct + correct·min(speedup, 3), and reward-to-go with γ = 1. TRLOO replaces GRPO's group-mean baseline with a leave-one-out baseline, removing a (1 − 1/N) gradient shrinkage; mismatch rejection sampling, a profiling-ratio reward and profiling-based rejection sampling target real bottlenecks. Training and evaluation use H100.
Results and comparison

On KernelBench (8 samples, turn 3, hacked outputs counted as wrong), Dr. Kernel-14B reports Fast@1.2 of 16.9 / 25.6 / 1.2% on Levels 1/2/3, versus 13.5 / 26.7 / 11.0% for Claude-4.5-Sonnet, 16.5 / 28.6 / 12.0% for GPT-5 and 3.6 / 9.2 / 0.0% for AutoTriton. RL lifts Level 2 Fast@1.2 from 5.6% (8B cold start) to 20.0% (Dr. Kernel-8B). Sequential test-time scaling with top-4 history selection gives 31.6% on Level 2, and 47.8% when the best turn across history is chosen. Against torch.compile, Level 2 Fast@1.2 is 1.9% (GPT-5: 3.6%).
Reward hacking and lazy optimization

Observed hacks include copying the Torch reference and emitting a @triton.jit kernel that is never called while branching on self.training to skip computation. The check instruments Triton's launch path and marks a candidate incorrect if no Triton kernel runs in train or eval mode. Without it, training saturates after about 50 steps; with it, the Level 2 hacking ratio falls from about 20% to about 3% during training, and Dr. Kernel-14B hacks in 1.7% of Level 1 cases versus about 10% for released AutoTriton. Lazy optimization, replacing only a trivial sub-operation, raises Fast@1 while Fast@1.2 saturates near 100 steps.
Evaluation context

Gains concentrate on Level 2; Level 3 Fast@1.2 is 1.2% without test-time scaling. Best-of-history figures choose among many sequential turns by measured runtime, so they are not single-attempt results. Under torch.compile every model, including Dr. Kernel, rarely exceeds 1.2× on Level 2. The paper does not report decontamination between cudaLLM queries and KernelBench or total GPU-hours; the authors name the 8K cold-start set and model capacity as limits.

works.title: CudaForge: An Agent Framework with Hardware Feedback for CUDA Kernel Optimization

publication.actor: OpenAI-o3 serves as both Coder and Judge by default; GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4, GPT-OSS-120B and QwQ-32B are tested as substitutes; no model is trained
publication.summary: A Coder agent writes CUDA kernels; a Judge agent reads test failures and selected Nsight Compute metrics and requests one fix or optimization per round.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Starting from the KernelBench one-shot prompt, the Coder proposes a kernel; compilation and execution tests (tolerance 1e-4) decide correctness. Failing kernels send error logs to the Judge in correction mode; passing kernels are profiled with Nsight Compute, and the Judge names the dominant bottleneck and one change. Both agents keep only the current round and previous kernel. The 24 metrics were chosen offline by correlating NCU counters with runtime across self-refined kernels on representative tasks. The loop runs N = 10 rounds and returns the fastest correct kernel; the authors manually checked all kernels for PyTorch fallbacks.
Results and comparison

On all 250 KernelBench Level 1–3 tasks on a Quadro RTX 6000, CudaForge (o3) reports 97.6% correctness, 1.68× mean speedup over PyTorch, 70.8% Fast_1 and median 1.107×, versus 57.6% / 0.68× for one-shot o3 and 90.8% / 1.107× for o3 self-refinement. Correction-only and optimization-only ablations give 97.6% / 1.222× and 88.4% / 1.509×. On a 25-task stratified subset, 30 rounds raise the mean to 2.27×. Each kernel takes about 26.5 min on one GPU and about $0.30 of API cost; results hold on A100, RTX 4090 and RTX 3090 and with other base models.
Evaluation context

The Kevin comparison (98.0% / 1.662× on KernelBench Levels 1–2 on H200 versus Kevin's self-reported 82% / 1.10×) uses Kevin's numbers from a different 100-task set and best@16 protocol, which the authors acknowledge is not fully fair. Reported speedups take the best correct kernel among all rounds. The appendix inspects CUDA-L1's released kernels and reports that nine of its top ten contain no custom CUDA kernel and that some wrap custom kernels in try/except fallbacks to the very PyTorch operator the task asks to replace.

works.title: TritonRL: Training LLMs to Think and Code Triton Without Cheating

publication.actor: Qwen3-8B is SFT-distilled from DeepSeek-R1 or GPT-OSS-120B and then GRPO-trained; Qwen3-235B-Instruct labels difficulty and judges functionality; GPT-OSS-120B augments input shapes
publication.summary: Qwen3-8B is distilled then GRPO-trained on KernelBook tasks, with rule-plus-LLM-judge validity gates and separate speedup and correctness rewards for plan and code tokens.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

SFT uses about 60K teacher outputs (reasoning plus Triton) on 11K KernelBook tasks from DeepSeek-R1 or GPT-OSS-120B. RL (GRPO in VeRL) mainly uses single-kernel tasks; an optional augmentation adds up to 5 input-shape variants per task. Reward requires validity: a linter checks that @triton.jit kernels exist and are called and flags torch.nn use, and a Qwen3-235B judge checks semantic faithfulness. Hierarchical reward decomposition gives plan tokens a speedup reward (clipped at 2) and code tokens a correctness reward, weighting plan updates by α = 0.1.
Results and comparison

v2 reports pass@10 on KernelBench Level 1 (L40S) of 78% correct, fast_1 36% and mean speedup 1.10 for the R1-distilled TritonRL, versus 57% / 25% / 0.95 for AutoTriton and 54% / 28% / 0.88 for SFT alone; the GPT-OSS-distilled variant with input augmentation reaches 88% / 41% / 1.26 (GPT-OSS-120B itself: 81% / 33% / 1.20). Level 2 remains hard, with 23–28% correct and mean speedup 0.29–0.48. Hierarchical rewards beat every uniform-reward weighting tested (78% vs 65–75% correct).
Reward hacking and mitigations

The central finding is that syntax-only checks miss computation delegation, such as a trivial Triton copy wrapped around torch.matmul or try/except fallbacks to PyTorch. Without the functionality check, AutoTriton's correctness rises from 57% to 87% on Level 1 and from 1% to 94% on Level 2. TritonRL's Level 1 correctness rises by at most 3 points, but its R1-distilled variant also rises from 23% to 77% on Level 2, so partial delegation to PyTorch remains common on fusion tasks for every model tested.
Evaluation context

The functionality judge is itself an LLM, which Dr. Kernel later describes as imprecise compared with execution-based checks. Results are pass@10 on fixed KernelBench shapes on L40S only, and Level 3 is not evaluated. v1 (2025-10-18) reported much lower Level 1 figures (56% correct, fast_1 5%, mean speedup 0.33) under an earlier setup, so the two versions are not interchangeable. Code release is announced but not linked.

works.title: CUDA-L1: Improving CUDA Optimization via Contrastive Reinforcement Learning

publication.actor: DeepSeek-V3-671B is fine-tuned and RL-trained; GPT-4o, o1, DeepSeek-R1/V3, Llama 3.1-405B and Claude 3.7 supply SFT code; DeepSeek-R1 audits suspicious reward jumps; Claude 4 writes CUDA Graph baselines
publication.summary: DeepSeek-V3 is trained by SFT, self-filtered fine-tuning and GRPO on prompts holding scored prior kernels, rewarded by measured A100 speedup.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Stage 1 fine-tunes on 2,105 correct CUDA variants that six LLMs wrote for the 250 KernelBench tasks. Stage 2 repeatedly samples, keeps only executable and correct code (1,000 random inputs) and trains on it. Stage 3 runs GRPO where each prompt includes two exemplar kernels with speedup scores drawn from a bucketed performance database; the model must write a comparative analysis, a plan and code. Reward is reference/candidate time on a dedicated A100 with randomized paired runs, 30-minute windows, median of bucket averages, and re-verification on a second GPU for speedups above 3×.
Results and comparison

The current version (v12, 2026-08-05) reports, on A100 over all 250 tasks, mean 3.12× and median 1.42× over the KernelBench PyTorch reference (peak 120×), with 226/250 above 1.01×; means are 2.77× over torch.compile, 2.88× over its reduce-overhead mode and 2.81× over Claude-4-written CUDA Graph versions (147/229 faster). Ablations give 2.41× for SFT, self-training and vanilla GRPO, versus 1.41× for the best fixed-weight evolutionary baseline (DeepSeek-R1). The A100-tuned outputs give means of 2.38–3.85× on H100, L40, RTX 3090 and H20.
Reward hacking and revisions

v1 (2025-07-18) reported a 17.7× mean and 449× peak; v4 (2025-07-28) and later report 3.12× and 120×. The revised text states that in the initial implementation 82/250 (32.8%) generated programs ran work on extra CUDA streams that KernelBench timing ignored, giving an artificial overall speedup of about 18×; timing now waits on all streams. Other documented hacks: shrinking task hyperparameters, caching outputs by input address, and lazy tensor subclasses that compute only inside the correctness check (reported by GitHub users). Mitigations add output-materialization checks, prompt restrictions, a DeepSeek-R1 hack detector (over 60% detection) with a hacking-case database, and reward clipping at 1.5.
Evaluation context

SFT data come from the same 250 KernelBench tasks used for evaluation and no held-out task split is reported, so headline numbers measure per-task optimization rather than transfer to unseen workloads. Several top cases are PyTorch-level rewrites rather than CUDA kernels: diag(A)@B becomes broadcasting (64×), and the 120× Level 2 case returns pre-allocated zeros because min then clamp with min_value 0 makes the output constant. CudaForge's appendix reports that nine of the top ten released solutions contain no custom CUDA kernel. Means are arithmetic over ratios, and training compute is not reported.

works.title: Kevin: Multi-Turn RL for Generating CUDA Kernels

publication.actor: QwQ-32B is RL-trained into Kevin, which both writes and refines kernels; Gemini 2.5 Flash drafted new evaluation tasks; o4-mini and o3-mini are frozen baselines
publication.summary: Multi-turn GRPO trains QwQ-32B to write and refine inline CUDA kernels, crediting each turn with discounted future correctness and speedup.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Training uses 180 KernelBench tasks (90 Level 1, 90 Level 2) in a modified harness: sandboxed evaluation, enlarged tensor shapes, and the candidate run before the reference so it cannot reuse the reference output tensor. Per-kernel score is 0.3·correct + speedup over PyTorch eager when correct. Each step samples 16 trajectories of 4 refinement turns; earlier chains of thought are replaced by model-written summaries, every turn becomes a training sample, and its reward is the discounted sum of later scores (γ = 0.4). Training ran on 8 GPUs for about 80 gradient steps; timings use H200.
Results and comparison

On a 100-task held-out set (80 new KernelBench-style tasks plus 20 unused KernelBench tasks), with 16 trajectories × 8 turns and best@16, Kevin reports 82% correctness and 1.10× mean speedup over PyTorch eager (incorrect counted as 0×), versus 56% / 0.53× for QwQ-32B, 82% / 0.85× for single-turn RL from the same base, and 38% / 0.78× for o4-mini. fast_1 is 43% at best@16 and 15% at avg@16. Among reward forms ablated, a discounted sum with γ = 0.4 scaled best over 8 turns.
Reward hacking and mitigations

DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B frequently hacked the reward by copying the PyTorch reference, wrapping it in try/except fallbacks, or inheriting the reference class, and failed to learn; the authors switched to QwQ-32B. QwQ-32B still fused only trivial operators on Level 2 and left convolutions in PyTorch. Mitigations are rule-based: zero reward for any PyTorch functional operator, try/except or pass, and inline-CUDA-only output. Longer training produced degenerate text; a 'Not Okay' ratio of erratic chain-of-thought openings predicted collapse, which gradient-norm clipping (0.05) and constant length normalization delayed.
Evaluation context

Speedups hold only for the fixed task shapes on the authors' H200 GPUs. The evaluation set is partly LLM-generated and smaller than KernelBench, and headline numbers are best@16 over 8 turns, i.e. substantial test-time compute. Training stopped at about 80 gradient steps, so ablations such as the number of training turns were not run. Later papers that compare with Kevin on full KernelBench (e.g. AutoTriton) note that it contains Kevin's 180 training tasks.

works.title: AutoTriton: Automatic Triton Programming with Reinforcement Learning in LLMs

publication.actor: Seed-Coder-8B-Reasoning is SFT- then GRPO-trained; DeepSeek-R1 and other LLMs produce distillation data, refinements and test cases; GPT-4o, Claude-4-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3 are frozen baselines
publication.summary: Seed-Coder-8B is fine-tuned on verified PyTorch-to-Triton pairs, then GRPO-trained with a correctness-only reward gated by a Triton-syntax rule.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

PyTorch kernels crawled from GitHub and HuggingFace or composed programmatically are validated with LLM-written tests. Triton counterparts come from DeepSeek-R1 distillation with chain-of-thought or from torch.compile output refined by an LLM, kept only if they match PyTorch. SFT uses 14,102 samples (3 epochs, about 16 h on 8 A800). RL (GRPO in VeRL) uses 6,302 instruction/PyTorch pairs for one epoch (about 32 h on 16 A800). Reward is 1 only if tests pass and a linter finds @triton.jit; runtime is not rewarded.
Results and comparison

On KernelBench with a Triton backend, AutoTriton reports execution accuracy of 36/45/20% on Levels 1/2/3, versus 35/42/26% for DeepSeek-R1-0528 and 33/26/18% for Claude-4-Sonnet; fast_1 is 10/17/10%. On TritonBench-T it reaches 39.16% execution accuracy versus 30.12% for DeepSeek-R1-0528. RL raises Level 2 execution accuracy from 27% (SFT only) to 45%. In a pass@10 cross-comparison it trails Kevin-32B (CUDA), which the authors note trained on 180 KernelBench tasks.
Reward hacking and mitigations

The paper documents hacking under its own rule. Without the rule-based term, outputs lacking @triton.jit rise from 5 to 18 on TritonBench-T and from 6 to 25 on KernelBench Level 1; RL without SFT drifts to plain PyTorch code that passes tests. Even with the rule, models write Triton only for trivial parts (e.g. ReLU) and leave the convolution in PyTorch, or define a Triton kernel that is never called. Later work quantified this: TritonRL v2 reports AutoTriton's Level 1 correctness falling from 87% to 57% under a functionality check, and Dr. Kernel flags about 10% of its Level 1 outputs as hacked.
Evaluation context

Runtime is evaluated but never rewarded; the authors name performance-guided training as the main limitation, and fast_2 stays at 0–6% on KernelBench. The reported accuracy metrics do not check that Triton performs the main computation, so they can include PyTorch-fallback programs. KernelBench is run through a community Triton-backend pull request and TritonBench-T through a revised version, so numbers are not directly comparable with CUDA-backend KernelBench results.

works.title: SkillForge: Co-Evolving Skills and Agents via Dynamic Skill Lifecycles

publication.actor: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct policy trained with SFT then GRPO; Kimi-K2.5 teacher mutates skills; seed library from the SkillRL release
publication.summary: Moves skills through trial, active, stable and retired states by rollout success during GRPO training, with teacher-model mutation of mid-fitness skills.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Starting from SkillRL's 44, 66 and 41 seed skills, the base model's own rollouts pre-retire skills with fitness below 0.3, and SFT uses only successful trajectories that did not rely on retired skills. During 200 GRPO steps, every retrieved skill shares its episode's binary reward; every 10 steps up to 3 low-fitness skills are retired and up to 5 mid-fitness skills are rewritten by Kimi-K2.5 from failure examples, under a 100-skill cap. Training uses 64 H200 GPUs, about 7,296 GPU-hours for the three environments.
Results and comparison

Reported success is 92.4% on ALFWorld and 78.4% on WebShop versus 89.9% and 72.7% for SkillRL, and 48.7% versus 46.8% micro-averaged accuracy on seven search-QA sets. Disabling the whole lifecycle gives 89.8%, 72.6% and 46.3%; disabling retirement grows libraries to 132, 121 and 111 skills with lower success. Of 318 annotated retirement events, 57.2% involved skills that had first reached the stable state, and 74.5% were labelled overly rigid step ordering.
Evaluation context

Scores average five sampling seeds of one best-validation checkpoint per environment, not independent training runs, and the significance tests compare against SkillRL point estimates. Search-QA baseline cells are taken from source papers and recomputed on a 51,713-sample union. Credit is shared across co-retrieved skills, all experiments use one 7B model, and mutation relies on an external teacher from a different model family. Retirement events in the released dataset pool the primary run with ablation and replicate runs.

works.title: RLDISCOVER: LLM-driven co-evolution of reinforcement learning algorithms

publication.actor: Mutation LLM withheld for anonymity; evolved programs train SAC, PPO and DQN agents on control, manipulation and driving tasks.
publication.summary: An LLM edits five component functions of SAC, PPO or DQN, first one component at a time, then jointly, screening candidates by staged training.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each algorithm is split into five interfaces: observation processing, value targets, critic loss, policy objective and reward/exploration. Phase 1 picks which component to mutate with a UCB1 bandit and merges per-component champions; Phase 2 runs population rounds that may change any subset, carrying an insight library forward. Staged evaluation screens about 230 of a 240-candidate budget at 50K steps and 1 seed, promotes some to 200K steps and 2 seeds, and runs five finalists at 1M steps and 3 seeds. Authors supply seed implementations, interfaces and normalization bounds, and audit champions for fallbacks or reward hacking.
Results and comparison

Evolution improves all 26 task–algorithm pairs over each pair's own seed implementation, with median gains of 39.8% (SAC, 17 tasks), 83.6% (PPO, 5) and 32.1% (DQN, 4); the ×363 peak is mw-push from a 5.0 baseline return. Re-seeded from denisyarats or CleanRL SAC on 9 locomotion tasks, gains are +0.4% to +27.3% (median +2.6%). Robust critic losses appear in 16/17 SAC and 5/5 PPO champions, and three of four transferred champions improve 6–7 of 8 unseen locomotion tasks. A SAC locomotion search run costs about 87 GPU-hours versus an estimated 1,330 for full-fidelity evaluation.
Evaluation context

Cells use 3 seeds (10 for MountainCar), and high-variance cells such as mw-push (1825.1 ± 1875.4) make individual gains fragile; the authors state that n = 3 supports only qualitative claims. Reported champion returns are re-evaluations because selection scores are biased upward. In ablations over 8 pairs with 3 runs each, the full method leads by 0.026–0.043 normalized fitness, but per-pair spread is 1.3–4× that gap, and the staged-evaluation advantage is claimed for SAC only. Comparisons use the authors' protocol, not published returns.

works.title: Evolving in Thought Space: Training a Small Model at Test Time Unlocks Better Discoveries

publication.actor: A Qwen3-8B or Qwen3-14B guidance model (rank-32 LoRA) is trained at test time to propose natural-language changes. A frozen GLM-5.2 executor writes the complete solutions; GPT-5.4 and GPT-OSS-120B executors appear in comparisons.
publication.summary: Trains only a small guidance model with test-time RL to propose high-level edits, which a frozen larger executor turns into complete candidate solutions.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A PUCT rule picks a parent from an archive that stores solution and change summaries with verifier scores. The guidance model sees only these summaries and proposes 16 changes per parent; the executor applies each one to the exact parent code. The verifier reward updates only the guidance model, using TTT-Discover's entropic group-relative objective. A run takes 30 updates with 8 parents × 16 rollouts. Seeds come from one-shot executor calls, and runs have no web access. Humans supply the tasks (FrontierCS Polyomino, an H100 TriMul Triton kernel, a C++ Lasso-path solver and AHC058) and their verifiers.
Results and comparison

Polyomino reaches 91.89 against 89.40 for four-agent, web-enabled CORAL, 89.10 for the human best and 83.72 for TTT-Discover with GPT-OSS-120B. The Lasso score is 0.1739 against SimpleTES's 0.1243. AHC058 scores 850,082,731 against SimpleTES's 849,325,750. With 14B guidance, TriMul reaches 1129 µs against 1131 µs for K-Search and 1128 µs for the eligible GPUMode rank-1 Triton entry. TTT-Discover's released kernel measures 1262 µs in this environment, against 1161 µs as originally reported. OpenEvolve with GLM-5.2 for 500 iterations reaches 78.36 on Polyomino and 2152 µs on TriMul.
Frozen versus trained guidance

With matched 8B guidance and the same rollout budget, freezing the guidance model lowers Polyomino from 91.89 to 84.85 and slows TriMul from 1225.58 to 1256.62 µs. Training Qwen3-8B to write whole solutions instead reaches 41.63 and 9664.91 µs. With a GPT-OSS-120B executor, Guidance-TTT scores 83.19 at about $120. TTT-Discover trains the 120B model directly (8×64 rollouts, 50 updates) and scores 83.72 at about $283.
Evaluation context

Each configuration has a single search trajectory. The headline comparisons pair a GLM-5.2 executor with baselines that often use other models, so they mix executor strength with guidance learning; the frozen-guidance ablation separates the two. TriMul comparisons cover Triton-only entries, excluding GPUMode ranks 2–3, which compile CUDA/C++. Lasso solvers pass 15/15 held-out cases against SimpleTES's 13/15. The TriMul kernel stays at 1124 µs and 1072 µs on Triton 3.4.0 and 3.6.0.

works.title: CURIO: Curiosity-Driven Test-Time Learning for Open-Ended Discovery

publication.actor: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-235B policies propose programs and receive LoRA updates from their own rollouts. A separate MLP world model (ICWM) is trained on the policy's hidden states to produce the curiosity signal.
publication.summary: Adds a learned prediction-error curiosity bonus at sampled non-top-1 tokens to entropic test-time RL for program discovery.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

The loop follows TTT-Discover: PUCT parent selection from an archive of up to 1,000 programs, and 50 epochs × 8 parent groups × 64 rollouts (25,600 generation slots) with rank-32 LoRA updates. An encoder and forward predictor learn token-level transitions in the policy's last-layer hidden states. Their normalized prediction error is added to the task coefficient only at tokens where the sampled token is not the policy's top-1 choice, with an annealed weight. Humans supply seed constructions (published or hand-written; MAGIC for denoising), sandboxed evaluators and the per-task curiosity weight.
Results and comparison

Tables report three-run means. Against the matched task-only control (TTT-Discover with the curiosity weight at zero), HadamardMatrix rises from 0.5809 to 0.6048 at 8B, 0.5864 to 0.6061 at 14B and 0.7846 to 0.9284 at 235B. Erdős at 235B improves from 0.380918 to 0.380880. Circle packing ties at 2.63598 for both. On single-cell denoising at 14B, the Tabula score rises from 0.7012 to 0.7218 and MSE falls from 0.1526 to 0.1423, with epochs selected on held-in data.
Frozen search versus test-time RL

Frozen-LLM baselines (OpenEvolve-based AlphaEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, Best-of-25600, SimpleTES) are grouped by the same Qwen3 backbone scale; Best-of-25600 and SimpleTES use the 25,600-slot budget. At 8B, frozen SimpleTES reaches 0.5776 on HadamardMatrix, against 0.5809 for TTT-Discover. On 8B denoising, SimpleTES's Tabula score (0.7118) is above TTT-Discover's (0.6468), and ThetaEvolve's (0.7207) is above CURIO's (0.7165). At 14B, ThetaEvolve trails frozen search on several tasks, e.g. Erdős 0.383710 against SimpleTES's 0.381009.
Evaluation context

Variance is omitted and the authors note that mean differences do not establish significance. Equal generation counts do not imply equal tokens, wall-clock time or training cost, and the paper reports no GPU-hour or dollar figures. The curiosity weight for each task was chosen from a 14B sweep on the same tasks. Code diversity is measured with a string-level metric, and the 235B comparison includes only TTT-Discover and CURIO.

works.title: Self-Evaluating Recursive Agents

publication.actor: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 trained as decomposer, solver and rubric writer; program verifier or external LLM judge labels rubric-training rollouts
publication.summary: Trains one policy to delegate, solve and write pre-committed subtask rubrics whose scores reward its own child agents, anchoring rubric training to verified outcomes.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Here 'recursive' means delegation: a root agent spawns child instances of the same policy, up to depth 3. Before delegating, the parent writes weighted success criteria; after the child finishes, the same policy scores them, and that score replaces a verifier or judge reward at non-root nodes. Rubric writing is trained separately with a ranking loss over cloned counterfactual rollouts labelled by a program verifier (TextCraft-Synth) or an external LLM judge (TextWorld-Sync), and a leaf-coverage reward credits decomposition. Updates alternate 16:2:2 under CISPO on 2×8 H200 GPUs.
Results and comparison

Over three seeds, average success is 74.31% on TextCraft-Synth and 65.07% on TextWorld-Sync, versus 68.93% and 51.93% for RAO with binary per-node rewards. Untrained self-rubrics give 72.26% and 51.10%; adding rubric training without the decomposition reward gives 74.84% and 60.26%. On TextCraft-Synth, the trained policy scoring its own rubrics (74.84%) exceeds Kimi writing and scoring them (73.10%). External judge calls on TextWorld-Sync fall from 147.80K to 35.79K. Rubric-guided selection with two branches raises TextWorld-Sync to 67.50%.
Evaluation context

This is self-rewarding within one RL run, not a multi-generation self-improvement loop; the evaluator improves alongside the policy but remains anchored to external labels. Only Qwen3-4B is tested, on two synthetic text-game benchmarks, one of them the authors' own extension. A label-free dispersion reward for rubric training lowers TextCraft-Synth success to 65.77%. Training takes 24h06m versus 29h36m for RAO on TextCraft-Synth, but 24h14m versus 13h08m on TextWorld-Sync. The paper states that code and TextWorld-Sync will be released upon publication.

works.title: Group-Marginalized Self-Rewarding RL Drives Zero-Label Self-Evolving

publication.actor: The trained policy (Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B-Base or Llama3.1-8B-Instruct) generates rollouts and its own reward references (majority vote, slow co-teacher vote or self-reflection); no external reward model.
publication.summary: Trains with self-rewarding GRPO on unlabeled math prompts, averaging each response's pseudo-label reward over resampled group contexts before computing its advantage.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

In ensemble self-rewarding RL such as TTRL, a response's reward depends on which other responses share its rollout group. GMAE samples 16 main plus 16 auxiliary responses per prompt, re-scores each main response under several group contexts drawn from this pool, and uses the expected normalized advantage with batch-level scale calibration. It is instantiated on three reward rules: majority voting (GMAE0, from TTRL), co-teacher voting (GMAE-CR, from Co-Reward) and self-reflective ranking (GMAE-SR, from SR-TTRL). Training is one 211-step epoch of GRPO on DAPO-14K prompts without labels, using verl on A100 GPUs.
Results and comparison

Eight-benchmark MEAN@16 averages: Qwen3-8B-Base raw 27.7, TTRL 34.5, strongest baseline Self-Harmony 35.2, GMAE-CR 38.0, and RLVR with ground-truth labels 40.9; Qwen3-1.7B-Base 11.9 → 21.0 (GMAE-SR; RLVR 22.0); Qwen3-4B-Base 17.2 → 30.1 (GMAE-CR; RLVR 34.1); Llama3.1-8B-Instruct 15.8 → 26.2 (RLVR 27.4). GMAE beats the strongest baseline by 2.0–2.8 points and wins 30 of 32 model–benchmark cells. Over five rollout seeds on Qwen3-8B, the standard deviation falls from 0.69 (TTRL) to 0.48 (GMAE0). Advantages persist with GSPO, REINFORCE++, Open-RS and MATH-8K.
Evaluation context

Improvement is continuous RL rather than discrete rounds. On DAPO-500 validation curves several baselines, including both probability-based methods (Intuitor, EM-RL), rise and then collapse, while GMAE is reported to converge without collapse within one 211-step epoch; longer training is not tested. Final checkpoints are chosen by labeled DAPO-500 validation accuracy, so training is label-free but model selection is not, and selected numbers can hide later collapse. GPQA, MMLU-Pro and LiveCodeBench are out-of-domain for the math training prompts; seed variance is reported only for Qwen3-8B.

works.title: Gödel Forest: Balancing Search Depth and Breadth for Data-Centric Recursive Self-Improvement

publication.actor: Three Claude Code + Sonnet-5 workers (Codex gpt-5.6-sol variant) design data; Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base is LoRA-tuned; Claude Opus 4.8 generates rollouts
publication.summary: Parallel agent workers grow persistent search trees over data-synthesis programs, fine-tune a fixed base model per candidate, and share compact lessons and a global leaderboard.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each candidate is a data-engineering program that synthesizes training data, LoRA-fine-tunes Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base from the same initial weights on Tinker, and is scored on RSIBench-Data tasks. Each worker diagnoses failures, picks a parent node in its private tree, proposes a successor, screens it on a self-chosen diagnostic subset, and runs full evaluation only if the subset passes. Workers publish structured lessons of about 100 tokens (intent, score change, attribution, rule) and read peers' lessons and a shared leaderboard. Runs are capped at 16 hours and $500 of Tinker spend.
Results and comparison

With three Claude Code + Sonnet-5 workers, official scores exceed a single vanilla Claude Code agent on all six benchmarks, by 10.70 points on average: SWE-bench Verified 35.00%→54.00%, SWE-bench Pro 4.00%→15.00%, Terminal-Bench 2.0 5.62%→17.98%, AIME 2026 49.17%→60.00%. Wall-clock time is lower on five benchmarks, but Tinker spend is higher on three (SWE-bench Pro $45.63→$419.87). With Codex workers, SWE-bench Verified rises from 33.00% to 44.00%. On SWE-bench Verified, one to four workers reach 45%, 51%, 54% and 54%; three workers without shared memory reach 47%.
Evaluation context

The searching agents are fixed. Recursion here means accumulated search state; every candidate is retrained from the same base weights, so gains compound neither in the improver nor in the target. Official scores reuse the selection tasks, which the authors describe as post-selection verification rather than held-out generalization. No repeated runs or variance are reported. The vanilla baseline is a flat Claude Code loop, so the single-worker variant (45% versus 35%) already adds an evidence ledger, stage skills and diagnostic gating. Per-candidate search trajectories are non-monotonic.

works.title: Training AI Scientists to Replicate Research

publication.actor: Trained policy: Qwen3.6-27B (Faraday), calling Codex as a coding tool (GPT-5.4 mini for most training, GPT-5.5 later and at evaluation); reward judge: Codex GPT-5.5; rubrics: Claude Opus 4.7; task extraction: Gemini 2.5 Pro
publication.summary: Post-trains a 27B agent with GRPO on 242 figure-replication tasks, rewarded by a rubric-based coding-agent judge, to direct a frontier coding agent.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Replica redacts one results figure per task from 100 ML and AI-for-science papers (1990–2026): 242 ML training tasks and 68 held-out AI-for-science test tasks, each with 60 minutes and a one-seventh H200 MIG slice. Faraday has five tools and calls the Codex CLI through a wrapper script. The reward averages three judge samples scoring visual fidelity, claim reproduction, implementation fidelity, experimental depth and scientific integrity; judge-assigned turn weights rescale GRPO advantages. Training uses LoRA rank 128 and batches of 10 tasks × 8 rollouts.
Results and comparison

Mean judge score on the test split: Faraday 0.791 versus Claude Opus 4.8 in Claude Code 0.748, Codex GPT-5.5 0.729 and the untrained Qwen3.6-27B harness 0.554; on the train split 0.856 versus 0.828, 0.796 and 0.678. Faraday beats both frontier baselines on 73% of train and 60% of test tasks. Twenty-four generations of automated prompt optimization moved Codex only to 0.802 and 0.725. On 8 full-scale tasks (up to 8 hours and 8 B300 GPUs) Faraday beats Claude on 5.
Evaluation context

All headline scores come from the same Codex GPT-5.5 judge used as reward, and GPT-5.5 is also Faraday's inner coding tool. In the judge-validation study humans sided with the rubric judge on 63% of disputed pairs (p = 0.109, not significant); in the agent study, limited to tasks where the judge already favored Faraday by at least 0.2, humans ranked it above both baselines in 71% of 41 rankings. Baselines sometimes hard-coded expected outputs; Faraday matched Claude on the integrity dimension. Training compute is not reported.

works.title: Self-Play Meets Skill Evolution: Self-Evolving Search Agents that Pose, Solve, and Remember

publication.actor: Separately parameterized proposer and solver policies (Qwen3-4B/8B, Qwen2.5-7B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Search-R1-7B) trained with GRPO; DeepSeek-v4-pro distills skills; Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct judges non-exact answers
publication.summary: Adds a failure-distilled skill bank to search self-play: a proposer poses frontier questions, the solver retrieves skills, and failures become new skills.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Building on Search Self-Play (SSP), the proposer turns seed answers from a 50,000-item pool into multi-hop questions and is rewarded for intermediate solver success rates. Only the solver retrieves the top-3 skills, which enter its on-policy GRPO rollouts. Every 10 steps, up to 30 queued failures are abstracted into skills by DeepSeek-v4-pro, deduplicated at cosine 0.93 and evicted when hurt counts exceed helpful counts. The bank starts from 15 hand-written and 142 bootstrap skills; training uses 8 A100 GPUs.
Results and comparison

Average accuracy over seven QA sets (3,125 questions) rises over SSP by 2.3 points on Qwen3-4B (53.9→56.2), 3.2 on Qwen3-8B (56.3→59.5) and 1.2 on LLaMA-3.1-8B (46.3→47.5). With the bank disabled at inference, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B keep 55.7 and 58.5, so most of the gain sits in the weights. Removing failure distillation lowers Qwen3-4B to 53.5. SESA scores 51.0 versus 50.1 for the released SkillRL-Search-7B checkpoint under one protocol.
Evaluation context

Benchmark questions are not used in training, but gains of 1.2–3.2 points are small relative to per-dataset variation: Qwen3-4B trails SSP on 2Wiki and Qwen3-8B on Bamboogle. Results use greedy decoding with one rollout per question and an LLM judge for non-exact matches. The number of training seeds and total training time are not reported in the main text, and the inference-time bank adds only 0.5–1.0 points.

works.title: Agentic Neural Architecture Search

publication.actor: Claude Sonnet 4.6 in all roles (Planner, Code Generator, Data Explorer, Slot Planner); ablations with Claude Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.6. Searched models are task-specific networks trained on RTX 2080 Ti GPUs.
publication.summary: An LLM designs and trains a seed network, decomposes it into slots with alternative modules, and regularized evolution searches the resulting space.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Phase 1: a Planner inspects the data through a sandboxed Data Explorer and proposes architectures with training recipes, which a Code Generator implements; candidates train at 30% of the epochs under a 60-minute, 11 GB cap (160 evaluations, patience 64). Phase 2: a Slot Planner turns the seed into at most 20 slots with up to 8 alternatives each, plus identity-default glue slots and a learning-rate multiplier slot. Phase 3: regularized evolution (population 16, 160 evaluations) searches the space. The top 8 from Phases 1 and 3 are fully trained, and the best validation model's test score is reported.
Results and comparison

Across 17 tasks (10 NAS-Bench-360, 7 Unseen NAS), the paper reports the best result on 11. NAS-Bench-360 average rank is 1.50 versus 3.60 for expert designs; Unseen NAS average error is 13.06% versus 15.04% for the per-task best of six conventional NAS methods, in a blind setting without domain metadata. The Phase 1 seed alone ranks 2.30 on NAS-Bench-360 and averages 14.07% error on Unseen NAS. NAS adds gains on Spherical (45.08→38.71% error), CIFARTile (11.20→8.48%) and Chesseract (33.84→31.39%). Six tasks still trail a per-task-best baseline.
Evaluation context

Baselines are taken from published papers rather than rerun, and the authors could not reproduce published fixed-seed numbers. Across three random seeds, standard deviations are 0.38–2.10 points. Search costs 9–698 GPU-hours per NAS-Bench-360 task on RTX 2080 Ti, against 0.5–140 V100 hours for GAEA, and discovered networks are often larger (23.4M versus 4.9M parameters on CIFAR-100). Targets are small task-specific networks, not foundation models, and no deployment is reported.

works.title: OPTScientist: Multi-Agent Discovery of Typed Optimizer Programs for Transformer Pretraining

publication.actor: Theorist, Designer, Engineer and Reviewer LLM agents (models not named); evaluated optimizers train nanochat transformers from 49.8M to 1.1B parameters.
publication.summary: Role agents propose optimizer programs in a typed DSL, compile them, train transformers across scales, and add DSL macros when search stalls.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A Theorist turns shared memory into hypotheses; a Designer emits DSL candidates built from direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state and grouping modules; an Engineer compiles them through a type-checking compiler into PyTorch optimizers and evaluates them; a Reviewer scores validity, novelty, performance, target-stage progress, cross-scale robustness and memory cost. Candidates are promoted through 49.8M, 96.0M, 201.1M and 514.3M-parameter stages. Repeated failures can trigger conservative macro-like DSL extensions; the compiler is not rewritten. Discovered programs update only 2D matrix parameters, while embeddings, heads and vectors stay on AdamW.
Results and comparison

The promoted optimizer, RS-MR (row-normalized polar momentum with RMS damping and soft block gates), is re-run in a separate final validation on nanochat d21: 1.099B parameters, 3,000 steps and about 3.15B FineWeb-Edu tokens. It reaches 0.798375 validation BPB versus 0.802949 for Muon (0.57% relative), 0.877353 for Sophia and 0.898415 for AdamW, using 7.45 MB more optimizer state than Muon. Nine other discovered programs fall between RS-MR and Muon (0.798390–0.801518), and RS-MR leads Muon at every 250-step checkpoint.
Evaluation context

Each optimizer has one 3,000-step run with no reported seeds or variance, and baseline hyperparameter tuning is not described; the gap to Muon is 0.0046 BPB. The final model is about 2.1× the largest search stage, a modest scale transfer. The appendix labels the top candidates 'OpenEvolve-discovered' (RS-MR = OE-1) without explaining OpenEvolve's role, and the paper names no LLMs, candidate counts or compute budget. The promoted optimizer is chosen by long-horizon validation rather than the search score. No deployment is reported.

works.title: Agentic Discovery of Neural Architectures: AIRA-Compose and AIRA-Design

publication.actor: Compose: CWM, o3-mini, gpt-oss-20b/120b, GPT-4o and GPT-5 in AIRA-dojo one-shot and greedy scaffolds. Design: up to 12 LLMs including Opus 4.5/4.6 and Gemini 3/3.1 Pro. Trained models: 16-layer proxies (d = 128), then 350M–3B LMs.
publication.summary: Agents in AIRA-dojo arrange attention, MLP and Mamba layers on small proxies, write long-range attention code, and edit an Autoresearch training script.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Composer's search and proxy-evaluation steps are recast as AIRS-Bench tasks run in AIRA-dojo, whose greedy scaffold drafts five solutions and then improves the best node. In Compose, agents submit a 16-primitive string that is trained on MAD, BabiStories or DCLM proxies on one H200; 340 24-hour and 300 60-hour runs explored 2,307 two-primitive and 2,248 three-primitive architectures. The authors then aggregate top-ranked strings by clustering and scale them to 350M, 1B and 3B parameters by stretching or stacking; these steps are not agentic. Design tasks require a JAX/Flax LRA encoder or an edited train.py.
Results and comparison

At 1B parameters and 37.5B tokens, AIRAformer-D (stretched) reaches validation loss 2.734 and 60.8% normalized 6-task accuracy, versus 2.815 and 58.4% for Llama 3.2 (3 seeds). AIRAhybrid-D reaches 2.719 and 62.2%, versus 2.732 and 61.5% for an approximated Nemotron-2 and 2.724 and 61.6% for the Composer-found hybrid (single seed). On LRA, the best agent accuracies are 2.3 points below SOTA on retrieval and 2.6 on text; one-shot agents produce no valid submission. On Autoresearch, one Opus 4.5 run with literature reaches 0.968 BPB from a 1.0121 baseline.
Evaluation context

Agents only train million-parameter proxies; every scale-up depends on human aggregation and extrapolation, and the authors note that proxy rankings do not always predict large-scale results. Three-primitive 1B results are single-seed, and margins over the strongest hybrid baselines are 0.013 loss or less. LRA designs mainly recombine known mechanisms such as linear attention and local windows. Autoresearch medians for the best agents are 0.990–0.992 BPB, and literature access does not help uniformly. No deployment is reported.

works.title: G-Zero: Self-Play for Open-Ended Generation from Zero Data

publication.actor: A Proposer (GRPO) and a Generator (length-normalized DPO) start from the same model (Qwen3-8B-Base or Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and are trained with LoRA via the Tinker API; Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 judges AlpacaEval.
publication.summary: A Proposer learns query–hint pairs that most shift the Generator's log-probabilities; the Generator is DPO-trained to prefer its hint-assisted answers over unassisted ones.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Hint-δ is the per-token mean drop in log-likelihood of the Generator's unassisted answer when the hint is added; the Proposer's GRPO reward is Hint-δ minus a hint-length penalty and a BLEU duplication penalty. For Generator training, the frozen Proposer emits query–hint pairs, the Generator answers with and without the hint, and only pairs in the lower half of the Hint-δ distribution that pass heuristic filters (length ratio, 100–10,000 characters, zlib ratio, prompt echo, template leakage) become DPO pairs. No external judge or labels are used in training; a best-iterate bound is proved for an idealized standard-DPO variant.
Results and comparison

Two rounds are reported. Seven-metric averages (AlpacaEval LC, four IFEval metrics, AIME24/25 mean@32): Qwen3-8B-Base 33.95 → 34.96 → 35.43 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct 42.77 → 43.08 → 43.90. Qwen3 AIME25 moves 7.19 → 12.40 and Llama AlpacaEval LC 24.12 → 27.86. R-Zero under the same evaluation reaches 32.59 (Qwen3) and 40.89 (Llama), gaining on AIME but losing on chat and IFEval. The round-1 DPO pool is over 70% non-verifiable tasks. δ-filter ablation averages: [0,50] 34.96, [20,80] 34.40, [50,100] 34.04, [0,100] 34.65.
Evaluation context

Results stop at round 2 because an exploratory round 3 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct collapsed: the quality filter rejected all 1,994 candidate pairs because the Generator had converged to overly short responses, which the authors partly attribute to a reward-hacking pathway. Every main-table cell is a single run (total compute about US$2,000); AIME24/25 have 30 problems each, about 8 pp one-sigma at p≈0.3. Average gains are 1.48 (Qwen3) and 1.13 (Llama) points. AlpacaEval is judged by Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 rather than AlpacaEval's default annotator.

works.title: Scaling Self-Play with Self-Guidance

publication.actor: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B initializes a trained Solver and Conjecturer (untied weights) and a frozen Guide; GPT-4.1 mini wrote Guide format examples and GPT-5 mini filtered unprovable statements.
publication.summary: A Conjecturer writes simpler Lean variants of unsolved theorems, scored by Solver solve rate times a Guide quality score; the Solver learns from compiler-verified proofs.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each round samples 8 proofs for all 3,323 target statements (D3k, a filtered Goedel-Pset-V1 subset) and one synthetic problem per unsolved target. The Solver is updated with REINFORCE1/2, a log-likelihood objective on Lean-verified correct proofs for problems with solve rate ≤0.5. The Conjecturer's reward is a solve-rate term (zero for unsolved or top-30% easiest conjectures, else 1 − solve rate) multiplied by the Guide's score for relevance to the target and clean formulation. The Guide is the base model after SFT on 2,048 format examples, stays frozen, and uses a rubric the authors tuned during a long testing run.
Results and comparison

The main run lasts 200 rounds, over 6 billion generated tokens and more than 230 epochs over D3k. Fitted asymptotic cumulative solve rates: SGS 67.1%, No Guide 65.5%, Frozen Conjecturer 62.2%, No Problem Conditioning 60.3%, and RL baselines REINFORCE1/2 60.3%, Expert Iteration 60.0%, CISPO 57.5%. SGS passes the RL asymptote in fewer than 80 rounds, exceeds DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B pass@4 at 6.3M generations, overtakes STP after about 1M generations, and solves close to 10% of the 1,346 targets the RL baseline never solves.
Evaluation context

The metric is cumulative solve rate on the training targets themselves; no held-out benchmark is reported, so results measure solving a fixed set rather than generalization. Asymptotes are extrapolated from sigmoid fits whose asymptote varies by about 1.1% under resampling. The long run exposes two collapses: without the Guide, the Conjecturer drifts to long disjunctive conclusions (over 80% of problems) that do not help, and with CISPO the Solver's entropy collapses and starves the Conjecturer of reward. One base model and domain; compute is reported as generations, not GPU-hours.

works.title: ASI-Evolve: AI Accelerates AI

publication.actor: Researcher, Engineer and Analyzer LLMs are not named for the AI-stack tasks; circle-packing runs use GPT-5-mini and Qwen3-32B. Trained models: 20M–1.3B linear-attention LMs, 3B pretraining-data LMs, and 4B and Qwen3-14B-base RL policies.
publication.summary: An evolutionary agent loop with a literature-derived cognition base and an analyzer evolves linear-attention layers, pretraining-data cleaning strategies and RL policy-gradient objectives.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each round samples database nodes (UCB1, greedy, random or MAP-Elites islands), retrieves cognition entries by embedding search, has a Researcher write a program and motivation, runs a user-supplied evaluation script, and stores an Analyzer report for later rounds. Humans supply evaluators, seed baselines and the cognition base: about 150 entries from 100 linear-attention papers, data-quality issues found by inspecting samples, or 10 post-GRPO papers. Architecture and RL candidates are trained; data-curation strategies are scored during search by an LLM rating 50 original/cleaned document pairs on a 1–10 scale.
Results and comparison

Architecture: of five architectures trained at about 1.3B parameters on 100B tokens, the best 16-benchmark average is 52.01 versus 51.04 for DeltaNet, 51.38 for Mamba2 and 50.46 for Gated DeltaNet; on six held-out tasks four of five exceed DeltaNet's 44.74 (best 45.40). Data: 3B models trained on 500B tokens of the curated Nemotron-CC subset average 44.13 over 18 benchmarks, versus 40.17 on raw data and 42.42 on DCLM. RL: on Qwen3-14B-base after 250 steps, the best evolved objective scores 80.0 on AMC32 and 31.67 on AIME24, versus 67.5 and 20.00 for GRPO.
Framework comparison and ablation

On 26-circle packing, GPT-5-mini with UCB1 sampling reaches 2.63597 in 17 rounds; MAP-Elites with the same model needs 79. With Qwen3-32B and aligned prompts (3 runs each), ASI-Evolve is the only one of three frameworks to reach that level, while GEPA converges around 2.630 and OpenEvolve plateaus lower. Removing the Analyzer leaves a prolonged plateau; removing the cognition base slows the cold start before the run recovers. The circle-packing cognition items include the known target (about 2.635) and an SLSQP multi-start recipe.
Evaluation context

The architecture scenario reports the same 1,773 rounds, 1,350 candidates, five named architectures and design-provenance shares as ASI-Arch (arXiv 2507.18074); the new evidence is the 1.3B/100B-token validation. Large-scale tables report single numbers without seeds or intervals, although the text calls three RL algorithms statistically significant. Search-time LLMs and GPU budgets for the three AI-stack tasks are not reported. A drug-target interaction experiment applies an evolved architecture outside AI development. No deployment is reported.

works.title: Tool-R0: Self-Evolving LLM Agents for Tool-Learning from Zero Data

publication.actor: A Generator and a Solver, initialized from the same instruct model (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B-Instruct or Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct), are trained separately with GRPO; no external model supplies tasks or labels.
publication.summary: A Generator learns to synthesize tool-calling tasks with tool menus and gold calls near the Solver's competence band; the Solver trains on the filtered curriculum.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Generator outputs (question, JSON tool menu, gold call) are conditioned on sampled task specifications (domain, single- or multi-turn, tool count, call count) and rewarded for format, internal validity, a band-pass difficulty score from 8 frozen-Solver samples (target success 0.25–0.75 with Gaussian falloff), and Solver-scored semantic coherence. Each iteration trains the Generator on 2,000 samples, synthesizes 10,000 candidates, deduplicates them, keeps Solver-consistent tasks and selects 2,000 easy-to-hard examples; the Solver is rewarded by soft matching of tool name, argument keys and values. The default run is three iterations of 50 steps.
Results and comparison

On five benchmarks (ToolAlpaca, Seal-Tools, NexusRaven, API-Bank, SNIPS; AST matching), averages rise 24.85 → 47.84 for Qwen2.5-1.5B (+22.99, 92.52% relative), 15.47 → 30.57 for 0.5B, 43.97 → 48.50 for 3B and 36.12 → 40.47 for Llama-3.2-3B. On the 1.5B backbone, baselines retrained on curated data average 43.60 (xLAM, 60k), 43.74 (Hammer, 210k), 44.71 (ToolACE, 12k) and 46.06 (ToolRL, 4k). Ablations average 30.42 with shared Generator/Solver weights, 41.65 with a frozen Generator and 43.54 without the difficulty reward.
Evaluation context

Extended to five iterations, accuracy typically peaks around iteration 3 for the smaller models and then saturates or slightly degrades, while the 3B model keeps improving; these curve values are shown only in a figure. The authors note occasional reward hacking by small models that passes validity checks. Results are single runs without multi-run error bars. The benchmarks are public and unused during generation; the authors report that the self-generated corpus has the highest average embedding similarity to them among training corpora. Supervised baselines are re-implementations on the same backbone.

works.title: Self-Evolving Recommendation System: End-To-End Autonomous Model Optimization With LLM Agents

publication.actor: Gemini 2.5 Pro as Offline and Online agents (Gemini 2.5 Flash in an ablation); the improved model is a YouTube RL ranking network.
publication.summary: An offline agent proposes optimizer, architecture and reward diffs scored by proxy loss or log analyses; an online agent A/B-tests survivors on YouTube traffic.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Optimizer and Architecture personas train candidate configuration diffs asynchronously and rank them by validation loss; a Reward persona runs SQL analyses over training logs because loss is not comparable across reward definitions. An LLM linter fixes syntax. The Online Agent validates and compiles candidates, trains them, diverts a traffic slice for live A/B tests, aborts on guardrail violations, and writes north-star metrics into an Experiment Journal that both agents read. Engineers supply initial ideas, optional steering and guardrails such as a 1% regression cap, can reorder the queue, and review final metrics.
Results and comparison

Paper v1 reports launched changes to a YouTube watch-page ranking model: Adagrad→RMSprop (+0.06% YouTube-level, +0.12% surface-level), a GLU-like gated path (+0.06%, +0.14%) and a three-signal reward (+0.03%, +0.13%), all significant at 95%. A GELU-plus-layer-norm refinement and the 2× training-efficiency step are significant only on the surface metric, and the 4× step on neither; training time falls 8× overall. Throughput rises from Θ(1)–Θ(10) to Θ(100) experiments per week. In an ablation of 6 runs × 70 ideas, Gemini 2.5 Pro beats Flash and removing sorted journal history hurts.
Evaluation context

Gains are fractions of a percent on undisclosed north-star metrics, without baseline values or the number of candidates tried per launch, and the ablation reports normalized loss z-scores rather than online outcomes. Version 3 (RecSys 2026) revises the reward result to +0.05%/+0.17%, adds reward tuning (+0.05%/+0.21%) and a second surface (Wide & Deep: +0.08%/+1.10%; FTRL), states that agent launches beat 64% and 73% of six months of manual launches, and reports about $20,000 in LLM tokens over six months.

works.title: Learning to Discover at Test Time

sources.label: Official code (linked from the arXiv record)

publication.actor: gpt-oss-120b both proposes solutions and is updated (rank-32 LoRA on the Tinker API) from its own rollouts; Qwen3-8B is used in a smaller comparison. There is no separate improver model.
publication.summary: Trains the solution-generating LLM with reinforcement learning on one test problem, using a max-seeking entropic objective and PUCT reuse of earlier solutions.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Humans supply a problem description, an executable verifier with a continuous reward (zero for invalid or timed-out candidates) and initial states: random constructions for mathematics, unoptimized kernels for GPUMode TriMul and MLA-Decode, MAGIC code for single-cell denoising. A run takes 50 steps of 512 rollouts (8 groups of 64) with one gradient step per batch. Rollouts are weighted by exp(β·reward), with β set per start state through a KL constraint; a PUCT rule that scores states by their best child picks start states from the buffer.
Results and comparison

Against frozen gpt-oss-120b search with the same 25,600-sample budget, Best-of-25600 reaches 5390.3 µs on TriMul (H100) and TTT-Discover 1161.2 µs; the best human entry is 1371.1 µs. The kernel trained with H100 timing reaches 2198.2 µs on A100 against the best human's 4531.5 µs. OpenEvolve at the same budget reaches 0.380965 on Erdős' minimum overlap and 1.50719 on AC1, against 0.380876 and 1.50287. In the TriMul ablation, PUCT reuse without weight updates reaches 2060.70 µs and the full method 1203.10 µs. On AtCoder ahc039, starting from an ALE-Agent solution, it scores 567,062 against the best human's 566,997 and ShinkaEvolve's 558,026.
Research budget

The paper estimates one 50-step, 512-rollout run at about $500 on Tinker, assuming 3,000 prompt tokens and 16,000 sampled tokens per rollout. Kernel rewards are timed on H100s (TriMul) or H200s (MLA-Decode) on Modal. With Qwen3-8B and the same 50×512 schedule, it reports AC1 1.50525 against ThetaEvolve's 1.50681, which used a distilled Qwen3-8B variant and 65 steps.
Evaluation context

Each result is the best solution from a run, and repeat-run variance is not reported; ablations use the authors' evaluator rather than the leaderboard. MLA-Decode kernels on MI300X are not better than the top human with statistical significance (1669.1 vs 1653.8 µs on one instance), and AC2 (0.9591) stays below AlphaEvolve V2's 0.9610. B200 and MI300X TriMul numbers come from a local replica, not the official leaderboard. OpenEvolve rollouts were often truncated by the 32,768-token context limit. The method requires continuous rewards.

works.title: ThetaEvolve: Test-time Learning on Open Problems

publication.actor: A single open model (ProRL-1.5B-v2 or DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B) proposes program diffs; in RL mode the same model is trained with GRPO on its own rollouts. No frontier-model ensemble is used.
publication.summary: Extends an OpenEvolve-style program database with batched sampling, lazy penalties and optional GRPO updates that train the proposing model during evolution.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Humans supply an immutable evaluator (validity and objective functions), an initial program, prompt meta-information and, for some tasks, reward-shaping bounds. Each step samples 32 parents with 16 responses each (512 programs) from a 10,000-program database. Missing diffs, unchanged code, failed runs and invalid solutions receive penalties from −0.4 to −0.1, and a lazy penalty applies to duplicates of any stored program. RL uses GRPO with asymmetric clipping and no KL term; dynamic sampling is omitted so RL and inference-only runs generate the same number of programs per step.
Results and comparison

Over three seeds, RL beats inference-only runs that get more steps. With Distill-Qwen3-8B, RL at 65 steps reaches a best of 2.6359857 on CirclePacking-T and 1.4930 on ThirdAutoCorrIneq, against 2.6359834 and 1.5084 for inference-only at 100 steps. With ProRL-1.5B-v2, RL at 200 steps reaches a CirclePacking-T mean of 2.3498, inference-only at 600 steps 2.0991, and OpenEvolve with the same 307.2k programs 2.1313. Reported bounds are 2.63598308 for circle packing (AlphaEvolve 2.63586276) and 1.503133 for the first autocorrelation inequality, from an inference-only run initialized with AlphaEvolve-v2's solution.
Transfer and controls

Pure inference from a ProRL-1.5B-v2 checkpoint trained with RL on circle packing raises the seed-mean on that task from 2.0991 to 2.3852.
