On unseen tasks it moves HadamardMatrix from 0.4920 to 0.5231 and ThirdAutoCorrIneq from 1.6766 to 1.6424. RL that always restarts from the initial program reaches 1.5985 against 2.3498 for RL in the evolving database. A format-only reward gives 1.6783 on ThirdAutoCorrIneq, slightly worse than no RL (1.6766).
Evaluation context

The comparisons match generated programs, not compute, because RL also spends training compute. The paper says experiments fit on 8×80 GB A100s and reports 5.4 h against OpenEvolve's 63.6 h for 204.8K inference programs on 4 A6000s. With ProRL-1.5B-v2 on HadamardMatrix, the 300-step inference-only mean (0.4920) exceeds the 100-step RL mean (0.4808). CirclePacking-T allows a 10⁻⁶ tolerance, and the corrected ThirdAutoCorrIneq evaluator is not comparable to AlphaEvolve's. All tasks are mathematical.

works.title: Language Self-Play For Data-Free Training

publication.actor: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct plays both Challenger and Solver; Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.2-3B supplies task rewards; the frozen initial model supplies self-rewards; Llama-4-Maverick judges AlpacaEval.
publication.summary: One model alternates between posing challenging prompts and answering them, updated with group-relative RL on reward-model scores plus a self-judged quality reward.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A challenger prompt makes the model emit N queries; for each, the same model samples G answers. The Solver's advantage is reward minus the per-query mean, and the Challenger is rewarded for queries with low mean reward, a zero-sum game (LSP-Zero) regularized by KL to the initial model. LSP adds a 7-point additive quality score from the frozen reference model to both players' rewards, so the game is no longer zero-sum. Humans supply the challenger and self-reward prompts, a task name per run and the external reward model; data is used only for evaluation.
Results and comparison

On AlpacaEval, win rates against a Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct copy are 26.5% for the base model, 32.0% for LSP-Zero, 36.4% for LSP and 38.8% for GRPO trained on Alpaca data; LSP followed by data-based GRPO reaches 39.5%. On test sets LSP recovers most of GRPO's gain: MATH 48.7 → 52.4 (GRPO 54.6), GSM8K 77.5 → 79.4 (79.8) and HumanEval 97.2 → 98.1 (98.7, GRPO trained on MBPP). Early runs with an OpenAssistant DeBERTa reward model degenerated into reward hacking, with the Solver answering most queries in Python.
Evaluation context

No performance curve over self-play iterations is reported; Box 4 only shows Challenger prompts at 500, 1,000 and 1,500 iterations. The authors state that with the self-reward term the play could run effectively indefinitely, without quantifying it. One 3B base model and one reward model are used, and no seed variance is reported. The authors attribute the limited gains to a mismatch between Challenger-generated queries and test prompts, and note that the ceiling is tied to the reward model's judgment quality.

works.title: R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data

publication.actor: A Challenger and a Solver, both initialized from the same base model (Qwen3-4B/8B-Base, OctoThinker-3B/8B), are trained separately with GRPO; GPT-4o grades benchmark answers and audits pseudo-labels in analysis.
publication.summary: A Challenger learns to pose math questions at the Solver's 50% uncertainty frontier; the Solver trains on majority-vote pseudo-labels, with no seed data.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each iteration first trains the Challenger with GRPO on an uncertainty reward, maximal when half of 10 Solver samples match the majority answer, minus a BLEU-cluster repetition penalty. The trained Challenger then samples 8,000 questions; those with 3–7 of 10 answers matching the majority vote are kept, and the Solver is trained with GRPO against those pseudo-labels. Humans supply the base model, a math-oriented Challenger prompt, the reward design and hyperparameters, but no tasks or labels. Built on EasyR1; v4 equates one iteration with 15 Solver training steps.
Results and comparison

v1 reports three iterations with monotonic math-average gains on all four backbones (seven benchmarks): Qwen3-4B-Base 42.58 → 48.06 → 48.44 → 49.07, Qwen3-8B-Base 49.18 → 53.39 → 53.84 → 54.69, OctoThinker-3B 26.64 → 29.32 and OctoThinker-8B 36.41 → 38.52; a Solver trained on questions from an untrained Challenger reaches 44.36 on Qwen3-4B. The overall average (math plus SuperGPQA, MMLU-Pro, BBEH) rises for Qwen3-8B 34.49 → 38.73, but for Qwen3-4B peaks at iteration 2 (34.92, then 34.64). Running R-Zero before GRPO on labeled math12k adds +2.35 points over labeled-only training on Qwen3-4B.
Evaluation context

The v4 iteration-scaling study runs a fourth iteration on Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B-Base and finds degradation at every scale: math averages peak at iteration 1 for 0.6B (27.39), iteration 2 for 1.7B (39.20) and iteration 3 for 4B (49.07, then 46.52). GPT-4o-audited pseudo-label accuracy on 200 sampled questions falls 79% → 69% → 63% over iterations 1–3 while question difficulty rises. Benchmarks are held-out public test sets graded by GPT-4o. v4 re-evaluates its main table (Qwen3-4B 42.57 → 49.93, versus 46.42 for Absolute Zero), so per-iteration values here come from v1.

works.title: AlphaGo Moment for Model Architecture Discovery

publication.actor: Planner: o3 and GPT-4.1; code checker and analyst: o3; training, testing and debugging: GPT-4.1; deduplication: GPT-4.1. Trained models are DeltaNet-style language models at about 20M and 340M parameters.
publication.summary: LLM agents evolve linear-attention layer code from a DeltaNet root, training each candidate and selecting by loss, benchmarks and an LLM judge.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Researcher, Engineer and Analyst modules share a MongoDB archive. Each step samples a parent from the top 10 and four references from ranks 11–50 of a top-50 pool, after a 200-run cold start without pool updates. Fitness averages sigmoid-scaled loss and benchmark deltas against DeltaNet with an LLM-judge score anchored at DeltaNet = 5 and Gated DeltaNet = 10. Proposals pass novelty, sub-quadratic and causal-mask checks; losses more than 10% below baseline are discarded as leakage. Humans supplied DeltaNet as the single seed, the FLAME training stack, the benchmarks and about 100 linear-attention papers distilled into a cognition base.
Research budget and scale transfer

Exploration ran 1,773 experiments on about 20M-parameter models (2,000 steps, about 1B tokens, 500 samples per benchmark) for about 10,000 GPU-hours. 1,350 candidates beat DeltaNet on both loss and benchmark at that scale. After filtering for complexity and parameter count, about 400 were retrained at 340M parameters on 1B tokens for another 10,000 GPU-hours. The 106 architectures the paper labels SOTA are those listed with lower final-step training loss and a higher 7-task average than Gated DeltaNet (42.10) at 340M/1B tokens. Only five were trained further, at 340M parameters on 15B tokens.
Results and comparison

At 340M parameters and 15B tokens, the five selected architectures average 48.18–48.51 over eight zero-shot tasks, versus 47.84 for Mamba2, 47.32 for Gated DeltaNet and 46.54 for DeltaNet; the best WikiText perplexity is 26.37 versus 27.08 for Mamba2. The headline 'scaling law for scientific discovery' is Figure 1: a cumulative count of the 106 architectures plotted against compute hours within this single run, described as linear without a reported fit. An LLM classifier attributes 44.8% of design components in the 106 to the system's own analysis, versus 37.7% for the remaining architectures.
Evaluation context

Each architecture has one training run at 340M parameters or less, with no seeds or confidence intervals, and SOTA membership is defined by training loss and benchmark scores at the same scale used for selection. The paper reports no component ablation, no comparison with a non-LLM search at equal compute, and no wall-clock or kernel efficiency for discovered layers, which lack optimized kernels. The linear count-versus-compute curve therefore does not separate the agents' contribution from compute spent. No deployment is reported.

works.title: Self-Rewarding Language Models

publication.actor: Llama 2 70B is both the trained policy and its own LLM-as-a-Judge; a fixed Llama 2-Chat 70B writes new prompts; Claude 2 drives early stopping; GPT-4 and the authors evaluate.
publication.summary: One model generates responses, scores them as its own LLM-as-a-Judge, and trains on the resulting preference pairs with iterative DPO.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

M1 is Llama 2 70B fine-tuned on 3,200 human-written Open Assistant instruction examples plus 1,630 judge-format examples built around an additive 5-point scoring prompt. Each later iteration samples 4 responses per new prompt, has the same model score each one 3 times, and keeps highest-versus-lowest pairs for DPO: 3,964 pairs train M2 and 6,942 pairs train M3. New prompts come from a fixed Llama 2-Chat 70B with 8-shot Self-Instruct prompting, not from the trained model, and DPO checkpoints are early-stopped with Claude 2 pairwise judgments on 253 validation examples.
Results and comparison

Two self-rewarding iterations follow the SFT stage. AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate against GPT-4 Turbo rises 9.94% (M1) → 15.38% (M2) → 20.44% (M3); MT-Bench rises 6.78 → 7.01 → 7.25 (SFT baseline 6.85). In GPT-4 head-to-head judging on 256 prompts, M3 beats M2 47.7% to 12.5%. The model's judging accuracy on held-out human Open Assistant rankings also rises, 78.7% → 80.4% → 81.7% pairwise (IFT-only SFT baseline 65.1%). A series trained without the judge-format data yields only 541 and 429 valid pairs and lower win rates.
Evaluation context

Gains are still increasing at M3, the last reported iteration; the paper does not test whether they saturate. Average AlpacaEval output length grows 1092 → 1552 → 2552 (as reported), which the authors note may affect judged quality. Gains are smaller on math and reasoning categories, and some NLP benchmarks drift down from M1 to M3 (GSM8K 60.27 → 57.70, ARC-Challenge 57.51 → 53.13, NQ 35.48 → 31.86). Instruction-following results rely mainly on GPT-4 judging; the human evaluation uses 50 prompts rated by the authors. One base model is studied.

works.title: Stateless Language Agents: Scaling Long-Horizon Automated Research

publication.actor: Advisor and Workers: Codex CLI with GPT-5.5 or Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8 (same model per run); an appendix pairs a GPT-5.5 Advisor with GPT-5.4 mini Workers
publication.summary: Keeps research state in the harness and rebuilds fresh, role-specific contexts so a stateless Advisor assigns experiments to parallel stateless Workers over 1B-token runs.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

No agent session carries over between invocations. Each epoch the harness gives the Advisor the task, the global best and a summary of outcomes by search direction that separates non-improvements from failed runs; each Worker trial sees only its assignment, its retained candidate and local feedback. Workers run under Landlock restrictions with limited network access, and protected evaluators score candidates outside their sandboxes. Tasks: four FrontierSWE ports, Anthropic's VLIW SIMD kernel take-home, three SOL-ExecBench GPU kernels and FrontierCS Structured-LWE; EvoX, CORAL and SwarmResearch share models, seeds and token counters.
Results and comparison

On the Anthropic kernel task with Codex at 1B tokens, SLA reports 1112.0 ± 8.9 cycles versus 1275.7 ± 133.9 for SwarmResearch (three runs each) and reaches SwarmResearch's final value at 67.9M versus 986.3M tokens. On FrontierSWE it trails the best baseline on all four tasks at 175M tokens but leads on all four at 700M, by 4.95 points on average. SOL-ExecBench scores rise 5.5% on average over the best baseline. The Advisor uses 0.24–0.51% of tokens versus 8.39–10.70% for SwarmResearch's Shepherd.
Evaluation context

Only the Anthropic kernel setting with Codex and the checkpoint ablations are replicated (three runs); other comparisons are single runs because one long run costs hundreds to thousands of dollars. Ablations resume from shared checkpoints for 100M tokens; removing Worker isolation costs 5–11 cycles there but 224 cycles over a full 1B-token run. Cost estimates exclude experiment-execution compute, and all tasks have executable evaluators. The paper also documents a CORAL run in which 98% of the final 1,500 sessions made no tool calls.

works.title: AgentDiscover: Autonomous Discovery with Minimal Search Scaffolding

publication.actor: A coding-agent CLI on Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Opus 5 or GPT-6 Sol (Claude Haiku 4.5 in ablations) plans the search and writes candidates; an optional meta agent writes skills; baselines use the same model in each setting.
publication.summary: Lets a coding agent direct the search, querying a graph database of past candidates, resetting context between sessions and reusing its own tools and skills.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

No selection rule is fixed: the agent issues read-only Cypher queries over a Neo4j graph of ideas, candidates, lineage and lessons (MAP-Elites or UCT selection is one query), runs local experiments, and submits candidates to an MCP server that scores them with a hidden evaluator and returns a steering message. When stalled, or when its context grows costly, a session ends and a fresh agent inherits the database, tools and skills; an optional meta agent turns transcripts into skill files. Humans supply the task, evaluator and budget.
Results and comparison

On Anthropic's kernel-builder take-home (simulated VLIW SIMD processor; Claude Opus 5, single runs) it reaches 960 cycles at $100 of model spend versus 1,098 for EvoX and 1,148 for CORAL, and 1,016 at $25. At matched spend it beats CORAL and TTT-Discover's published results on all nine multi-domain tasks, e.g. TriMul 2,080 μs versus 2,419 and 2,198 on A100. On 11 ADRS systems and math tasks with Claude Opus 4.6 and at most 100 candidates, it matches or exceeds published baselines, e.g. transaction scheduling 4651 versus 4566 for CORAL.
Evaluation context

Every main-table entry is one run, so no variance is reported. ADRS baselines are numbers published by CORAL under a 100-candidate cap, which does not count the agent's unsubmitted local experiments. Porting evaluators exposed exploits: a two-sample output scored 0.9259 on signal processing (corrected best 0.7948), a constant table scored 0.994 on LLM-SQL, and EPLB candidates read hidden workloads or hardcoded printed inputs (0.153→0.201). Its own claims use corrected evaluators; five-run ablations cover context resets, parallel agents and meta guidance.

works.title: FrugalEvo: Towards Cost-Aware LLM-Guided Program Evolution

publication.actor: A high-cost model (GPT-5.6 Terra or GLM-5.3) analyzes the task and proposes strategies; a low-cost model (GPT-5.6 Luna or GLM-5.3 Flash) implements and refines code; baselines use the high-cost model alone.
publication.summary: Splits program evolution between a strong model that proposes strategies and a cheap model that implements and refines them, under fixed dollar budgets.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

After a cold start in which the cheap model refines the seed program until it stalls, the strong model analyzes the task and evaluator once and then proposes K strategies per round; the cheap model implements each, ranks them by score and refines the best with sequential feedback until an attempt beats the incumbent. Island-based MAP-Elites stores programs and strategy history, and prompts place stable content first to raise prompt-cache hits. The paper also defines BA-AUC, the area under the best-so-far score curve over cumulative LLM cost.
Results and comparison

Three runs per cell, with $2/$1 budgets for math/systems tasks (GPT pair) and $1/$0.5 (GLM pair). FrugalEvo reports the highest mean BA-AUC on all five math tasks and on four of five ADRS systems tasks, e.g. signal processing mean 0.77791 versus 0.72031 for AdaEvolve (GPT pair). On circle packing it reports 2.635996 for $1.68 (GPT) and 2.635990 for $0.55 (GLM). On 10 ALE-Bench-Lite tasks at $1 it averages 1924.9 versus 1887.5 for OpenEvolve. Using either model for both roles lowers mean scores in ablations.
Evaluation context

Budgets are matched in LLM dollars, but baselines run a single model, so the comparison bundles model routing, prompt caching and search changes; evaluator and CPU costs are excluded. The circle-packing solution applies small radius increases within the evaluator's tolerance. With three runs, several systems-task differences fall within one standard deviation. Prices are list prices retrieved on 2026-09-04, and AlphaEvolve figures are reported values of unknown cost.

works.title: SEDIMA: Cross-Run Hierarchical Insight Memory for Evolutionary Search Agents

publication.actor: One backbone per run (GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3 Pro, Qwen 3.7 Max or Qwen 3 Coder) mutates programs, distills insights and synthesizes recommendations; Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds insights.
publication.summary: Distills evaluation traces into clustered natural-language insights that persist across runs and problems and are retrieved into OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve mutation prompts.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

After each evaluation the module stores a raw trace, has the LLM write a problem- or change-level insight, and assigns its embedding to a cluster represented by an attention-weighted centroid. Before each mutation it retrieves up to 3 clusters × 3 insights (2,500-token cap) and inserts three synthesized recommendations into the prompt. Selection, population and mutation logic of both harnesses are unchanged. Memory is pre-populated from problems disjoint from the evaluation set and keeps updating online.
Results and comparison

With 100 evaluated candidates per run, adding the memory raises AlgoTune harmonic-mean speedup from 1.64→1.73 (OpenEvolve) and 1.69→1.77 (ShinkaEvolve), averaged over five backbones, and ALE-Bench Lite average performance from 1094.3→1173.6 and 1133.1→1201.9; all 20 model–harness–benchmark cells improve. Warm same-benchmark memory beats an empty store (1.75 vs 1.67 on AlgoTune; 1187.8 vs 1113.7 on ALE-Bench), other-benchmark memory gains less (1.70; 1146.5), and random retrieval stays near no memory (1.62 vs 1.61 on AlgoTune-20).
Evaluation context

Main-table cells are single runs; ablation, transfer and per-step curves use three seeds. Budgets match evaluated candidates, not LLM calls, tokens or dollars, although the module adds a distillation call per write and a synthesis call per retrieval, so the reported 32.3% fewer iterations to reach baseline-best is not a compute saving. No other memory-based evolutionary system is compared. ALE-Bench budgets are smaller than leaderboard submissions, so absolute scores are comparable only within the study.

works.title: CollabFlow: Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Collaboration

publication.actor: Qwen3.5-9B as trainable Collab-Director and as frozen executor; six other frozen executors in transfer tests
publication.summary: A trainable director designs agent teams and message protocols for a frozen executor and is retrained each round on its own team outcomes.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

The Collab-Director selects agents from fixed profiles, binds library skills, and labels edges with one of three communication protocols. Within a team, a receiver adopts a differing answer only when the sender's evidence (an executable check outranks retrieval support, which outranks assertion) is stronger by a margin. Across rounds, Collaborative Trajectory Balance, a GFlowNet-style objective, retrains the director toward a reward-proportional distribution over teams. The reward multiplies the answer score by a smoothed success rate from the loop's own records and a description-length prior. Library skills are added, modified or deleted between evolution steps.
Results and comparison

Six in-distribution datasets train the director and six are held out, with 128 items each (30 for AIME 2026) and five runs. Mean in-distribution accuracy is 89.15 versus 84.78 for the strongest baseline (an evolving orchestrator) and 55.81 for direct Qwen3.5-9B. Out of distribution, EM is 69.92 versus 66.41 (evolving orchestrator) and accuracy 86.41 versus 83.83 (FlowSteer). The trained director also raises averages for six other frozen executors. In a one-run ablation, removing retraining across rounds costs 7.6 in-distribution and 13.6 out-of-distribution points.
Evaluation context

The executor, agent profiles, evaluator and update rule stay fixed; only the director, skill library and reliability records change, which the authors call a bounded form of recursive self-improvement. The main text does not state the number of rounds. Multi-round evidence is a one-run ablation, a training curve and a persistence check (15 of the 20 largest one-step gains remain five steps later), not a per-round held-out curve. Evaluation sets are small. An untrained director already lifts ALFWorld from 33.59 to 82.81, so much of the gain over direct inference comes from the multi-agent architecture.

works.title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution

publication.actor: DeepSeek-V4-Pro as both Solver and Editor; Qwen3.6-Plus for visual observations; all weights frozen
publication.summary: The frozen answering model revisits training videos to diagnose failures, edits its own harness code, and keeps revisions that improve accuracy within frame-cost bounds.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Video-RSI evolves an executable video question-answering harness (prompts, tools, observation memory and control flow) around frozen models. Before editing, the Editor queries the original training videos at new time ranges, sampling densities or modalities to test competing failure explanations. A gate accepts a candidate if accuracy rises with at most 10% more frames, or if frames fall by at least 20% with at most one fewer correct answer. Evolution uses 216 LVBench questions for revision and 72 video-disjoint questions for private selection over 20 revision attempts; the Editor sees only aggregate selection feedback.
Results and comparison

The harness evolved on LVBench is frozen and tested on MLVU, LongVideoBench, Video-MME and EgoSchema. Against the initial harness, MLVU accuracy rises from 62.4% to 72.9% while frames per question fall from 68.5 to 61.1; across the four benchmarks frames fall 10.8–44.1%. Against VideoSeek and VideoHarness-RSI reproduced with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, accuracy is higher on all four (MLVU 72.9% versus 68.1% and 64.1%), with fewer frames except versus VideoSeek on Video-MME (21.6 versus 17.8). Trace-only revision reaches 64.7% on MLVU; an accuracy-only gate reaches 67.1% with 81.9 frames.
Evaluation context

Only the harness changes; the Editor model and its revision procedure stay fixed. Five of 20 revisions are accepted, versus three for trace-only revision. Retrospective MLVU scores of accepted versions show the first accepted revision lowering MLVU accuracy despite improving development metrics, with most of the final gain from the last two accepted revisions. One evolution run is reported, without seeds or Editor cost. Other baseline rows are copied from publications that use different models. Frame counts exclude offline Editor observations and do not measure total compute.

works.title: R² Flow: Recursive Self-Improvement via Recursive Skill Evolution

publication.actor: Qwen3.5-9B Supervisor trained with a trajectory-balance objective; frozen Qwen3.5-9B executor; six other frozen executors in transfer tests
publication.summary: Alternates flow-based training of an orchestration policy with verifier-gated edits to the skill library it uses, so each phase trains on the previous phase's library.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A Supervisor orchestrates skills for a frozen executor on a graph that merges histories differing only in the order of independent steps, trained with a trajectory-balance objective (R²TB). Each skill gets a flow-share readout and a signed utility. Independent verifiers (unit tests, schema validation, assertions, execution status) label skill invocations into Beta posteriors; rule-based operators refine, split, prune, consolidate or generate skills only when credible bounds support it, and each edit must pass paired non-inferiority validation on a separate query set. A plateau in residual variance ends each phase.
Results and comparison

Over five runs on six in-distribution and six held-out datasets (128 items each; all 30 AIME 2026 problems), mean accuracy is 79.47 versus 73.90 for SkillOpt in distribution and 78.63 versus 75.78 for Trace2Skill out of distribution; direct Qwen3.5-9B scores 52.62 and 49.80. The mean primary score on held-out datasets rises from 71.2 to 81.02 over eight phases with one dip, and 33 of 37 committed edits raise the held-out verified score. With reward-derived labels instead, 25 of 44 edits raise training reward but lower the verified score, and accuracy peaks at phase 3.
Evaluation context

Both the Supervisor weights (inner loop) and the skill library it uses (outer loop) change, while verifiers, executor and edit rules stay fixed. Eleven of twelve deliberately injected harmful skills are pruned. Evaluation sets are small fixed draws, and the per-phase curve is one summary series. A training step costs 2,587 GPU-seconds, 7.5% more than GRPO, but total run cost is not stated. CollabFlow, from the same group, reports different direct Qwen3.5-9B scores on shared datasets (HotpotQA EM 46.25 versus 57.97 here), so numbers are not comparable across the two papers.

works.title: ScienceBuddy: Recursive-in-Recursive Self-Improvement for Interactive Scientific Agents

publication.actor: Qwen3.5-4B task model trained with GRPO; fixed GPT-6 Astra diagnoses and edits the harness; Qwen3.8-27B simulates researcher replies in the harness study
publication.summary: Alternates harness edits by a fixed auxiliary model with GRPO training of the task model under the selected harness, using rubric-scored scientific tasks.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

ScienceBuddy is a released biomedical research workspace with 224 tools in 22 modules. Researcher requests and replies are converted into Harbor tasks with weighted rubrics, scored by executable checks and a fixed judge. The inner loop keeps the task model fixed while GPT-6 Astra proposes one bounded instruction, skill or context edit, accepted only if the mean rubric score on paired development tasks strictly rises. The outer loop calibrates and augments task environments, then trains the task model with GRPO under the selected harness. Quantitative studies draw on 895 LAB-Bench and Biomni-Eval1 tasks in four families.
Results and comparison

In the coupled study, Qwen3.5-4B runs three cycles of ten harness steps and twenty RL updates. Harness validation accuracy rises within cycles from 38.9% to 44.4%, 34.4% to 46.7%, and 61.1% to 70.0%. Held-out single-attempt accuracy rises from 42.2% to 73.3%, with 33.3% of problems newly solved and 2.2% lost. Separately, harness adaptation alone over 288 conversations raises validation accuracy from 31.1% to 51.1%, and RL alone under the initial harness raises pass@4 from 48.3% to 67.8%.
Evaluation context

The coupled run reports no harness-only or RL-only control on its held-out set, no seeds and no test-set size; its section heading says two cycles while the text and figure describe three. Cycle 2 starts at 34.4% validation accuracy, below cycle 1's 44.4% endpoint, so inherited gains are not monotone. The paper notes that its editor stays fixed, so better task performance does not show a stronger improvement mechanism. Quantitative feedback is simulated; real researcher interactions are shown only qualitatively. The two component studies use different metrics.

works.title: AlgoEvo: Self-Evolving Agentic Search for Automated Algorithm Discovery

publication.actor: One LLM agent (GPT-4o-mini on TSP and CVRP, DeepSeek-V4-Flash elsewhere) inspects, diagnoses, edits and evaluates heuristic code, writes experience cards and refines its own design-skill documents. Baselines use the same backbones.
publication.summary: Replaces fixed evolutionary pipelines with an agent that edits heuristic code, records experience cards in a UCB tree and refines reusable design skills.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each task fixes initial code, the evolvable units, an evaluation function and an evaluation budget. The agent chooses among read, edit, diagnose, retrieve, evaluate and commit actions. Diagnosis uses hand-designed situation categories and counterfactual probes that neutralize one or two components. Every evaluation becomes an experience card in a task tree searched with UCB. Once a skill owns at least two trees, the agent rewrites that skill document from them. The authors supply the paradigm skills, plus six method skills built from EoH, ReEvo, FunSearch, MEoH, NSGA-II and MOEA/D. Counters invalidate runs that score candidates outside the shared evaluator.
Results and comparison

All methods run on LLM4AD with three seeds and a 500-evaluation cap. On TSP, AlgoEvo reaches a test tour length of 7.007 with 39 evaluations and 2.9M tokens, against 7.337 for MCTS-AHD at 500 evaluations. On CVRP it reaches 24.150 with 35 evaluations, against 25.950 for ReEvo. Bi-TSP hypervolume is 0.827 against 0.760 for MEoH. On Bi-FJSP its IGD (0.162) is worse than MEoH's (0.143). On CVRP-DR it reaches 8.999 with 271 evaluations and 139.2M tokens, against 9.112 for Synergy using 289.6M. On FJSP four-operator design it reaches 1927.5 against MOTIF's 1952.0.
Persistence and transfer

With the same budget per round, successive rounds lower TSP tour length from 4.8928 to 4.7995 and raise Bi-FJSP hypervolume from 0.1549 to 0.1862. Moving experience from CVRP to CVRP-DR lowers cost from a cold start's 10.314 (±0.345) to 9.816 (±0.642). Warm-starting TSP improves the mean from 4.961 to 4.808. In a separate CVRP-DR batch, removing the experience bank, the skill hub or situation-triggered injection raises cost by 0.66%, 0.58% and 0.21%.
Evaluation context

The six tasks are combinatorial-optimization heuristics, not AI-development artifacts; the paper is relevant as a self-modifying search procedure. Multi-objective rows report training-instance quality. The warm-start test uses a different plain-TSP configuration, and the ablation is a separate batch. The authors note that skills are refined by after-the-fact summarization without held-out validation and may overfit related task distributions. Situation categories are hand-crafted. Cost is reported as evaluations and tokens, not wall-clock time or dollars.

works.title: Auto-RecSys: Harnessing Autonomous Research Agents for Industry-Scale Recommender System

publication.actor: Unnamed LLM agents operating Meta's recommendation-model training infrastructure; the changed artifacts are recommendation-model experiments and the agents' own playbooks.
publication.summary: Agents run parallel multi-day recommender experiments and rewrite per-model playbooks of dead ends and submission recipes that later sessions read.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A finite-state machine moves each idea through ideating, implementing, validating, training, debugging and analyzing, with one state file per idea in a shared store so sessions on other servers can resume work. Natural-language skill files guide reasoning while deterministic scripts perform state transitions, API calls and job submission. An Execution Evolution Loop distills trajectories into model-specific playbooks (dead ends, pipeline recipes, submission configurations); an Idea Evolution Loop logs positive, neutral or negative verdicts against a shared baseline and ranks ideas from researchers, literature or the agent. Interactive mode pauses for idea selection and code review.
Results and comparison

On one model over 31 iterations, major operational fix steps fall from 4.0 per iteration (iterations 1–4) to 1.3 (iterations 5–20). A baseline change at iteration 21 forces five consecutive recovery iterations, after which iterations 26–31 average 0.5, with 5 of 6 needing no fix. In one session the agent runs 970 log entries and 110 tool calls without intervention. In another it replaces monitor agents that died from context overflow with a cron-based design and submits that change to its own orchestrator.
Evaluation context

The paper reports no recommendation-quality metrics, launches or compute figures; outcomes are operational fix counts from session transcripts and a qualitative estimate that attention once spent on one idea now covers more than a dozen. The reliability analysis covers one model without a control harness, and the LLM is not named. Playbook updates are accepted on agent judgment without a validation gate. In autonomous mode, humans still select ideas and handle escalations.

works.title: WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution

publication.actor: Inference and skill-source models: Qwen-3.5-4B, Qwen-3.5-9B, Qwen-3.6-27B, Gemma-4-31B and Gemini-3.5-Flash; the paper does not name a separate backbone for the Wiki Maintainer and Skill Proposer
publication.summary: Co-evolves agent skills with a persistent wiki of failure patterns and proposal history, accepting skill edits only when validation accuracy improves.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each iteration runs the inference agent on the training split with active skills injected in full. A Wiki Maintainer consolidates up to 8 sampled traces (at most 5 failing, 3 passing) into pattern pages and logs, and a ReAct Skill Proposer reads the wiki, a skill-impact log and raw traces to make one atomic skill creation or edit. The edit is kept only if the validation score strictly improves; rejected skills roll back but the wiki never does. Splits follow EvoSkill and SkillOpt, with 16–80 training tasks per benchmark and iterations 0–7.
Results and comparison

Averaged over five benchmarks, WikiSkill exceeds the strongest of Trace2Skill, EvoSkill and SkillOpt by 3.3–12.0 points per model. Gemini-3.5-Flash moves from 49.5 (no skill) and 56.1 (EvoSkill) to 68.1, and Qwen-3.6-27B from 39.4 and 53.3 to 63.3. In the Gemini-3.5-Flash ablation, removing the wiki from the proposer lowers the four-benchmark average from 63.7 to 48.7, and giving the inference agent wiki access during rollouts lowers it to 60.9.
Evaluation context

Scores average three full evolution runs on held-out test splits with paired bootstrap tests. Validation splits are small (10–40 tasks), and Gemini-3.5-Flash reached 100% validation on ALFWorld before evolving, so no skill was learned there. Negative transfer appears: Qwen-3.5-4B skills lower its own OfficeQA score from 30.2 to 28.5 and drop Gemini-3.5-Flash on SpreadSheet from 50.5 to 18.1. Skills bypass retrieval through full injection, the wiki is never pruned, and optimizer token or dollar cost is not reported.

works.title: Recursive Experiential–Working Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agent Harnesses

publication.actor: Fixed Meta-Agent built on Claude Code (re-implemented on DeepSeek Harness); doubao-seed-2-0-pro is the deployment model during evolution; ten frozen target models including GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5 and Qwen3.6-27B
publication.summary: A fixed Meta-Agent localizes failures to skills, working-memory schema, invocation policy or checkers and admits scoped patches through a regression gate.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Working memory tracks goals whose completion must be confirmed by checker predicates on tool output, and skills are injected at tool-call or turn-boundary events according to that state. Structured traces of failed episodes from an evolve split go to the Meta-Agent, which assigns each failure to one of four memory components and patches only those. A fixed gate admits a patch only if it repairs the source failure without exceeding a preset regression on a dev split containing anchor tasks. τ²-Retail uses 16 evolve, 12 dev and 86 held-out tasks.
Results and comparison

Recuris improves 35 of 37 completed model–benchmark pairs (avg@4). A package evolved on doubao-seed-2-0-pro raises that model on τ²-Retail from 58.1 to 81.4 and transfers to GPT-5.6 Sol (58.3→76.1) and Claude Opus 5 (72.4→87.9). On the 86 held-out retail tasks, evolved packages beat the empty starting memory by 9.01–17.44 points. Keeping the whole skill library in context scores 65.57% versus 83.55% for state-grounded invocation, at 146,849 versus 100,865 tokens per success.
Evaluation context

Evolution draws on 16 retail training tasks, and SkillFlow has no held-out task split, so its gains measure cross-model transfer only. Two τ²-Airline lineages show no held-out gain, Gemini 3.7 Flash loses 1.5 points on Airline, and cross-task evolution on Terminal-Bench 2.1 admitted no patch in thirteen runs; there, retries account for the +26.4 headline and adaptation adds 2.3 points (p = 0.774). The memory only grows (51 skills added, none deprecated), and dollar cost is unavailable.

works.title: EVO-HARNESS: Context-to-Harness Skill Compilation for Self-Evolving Agents

publication.actor: Claude Opus 4.6 as default solver and evolver; Claude Sonnet 4.5 selects skills; Opus 4.7, Opus 4.5, Kimi-K2.5 and GPT-OSS in model ablations
publication.summary: Reflects on failed executions in a task stream and has an LLM evolver merge lessons into a capped Markdown skill harness for a frozen solver.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Tasks arrive in batches of 16. A Sonnet 4.5 selector injects relevant harness skills, the frozen solver runs, and failed or negatively scored executions are reflected into candidate lessons with trigger, evidence and scope. After each batch the evolver adds, merges, revises or skips candidates, keeping at most 5 general skills and 5 skills per task-type topic. Feedback comes from the benchmarks: Docker verifiers, repository tests, state checks and a CL-Bench rubric judge.
Results and comparison

With Opus 4.6, No-Evolve→Evo-Harness success is 29.54→34.02 on CL-Bench, 62.92→73.03 on TerminalBench-2, 63.67→67.00 on SWE-bench Lite, 72.73→76.97 on τ-bench and 72.50→76.25 on WebArena-Infinity. The strongest baseline, XSkill, scores 31.44, 66.29, 64.67, 73.94 and 73.75. Several baselines (AWM, Dynamic Cheatsheet variants, ACE) fall below No-Evolve on some benchmarks. CL-Bench gains are +3.7 to +4.5 for Claude Opus solvers but +1.1 and +0.8 for Kimi-K2.5 and GPT-OSS.
Evaluation context

Main scores are online: each task is solved with the harness compiled from earlier tasks in the same stream, averaged over three runs. A train-split transfer test on SWE-bench Lite (68.8 No-Evolve, 73.4 transfer, 75.0 online) is the held-out check. Self-generated feedback falls below No-Evolve on CL-Bench (27.96) and SWE-bench Lite (61.67), and a Sonnet 4.5 solver ends below No-Evolve with either evolver (55.3 and 55.7 vs 58.0). Total API spend across all experiments was on the order of $100K.

works.title: AI Research Preference Models

publication.actor: End-to-end: Qwen3.6-27B for both AIRA-dojo operators and the frozen RPM; offline studies: GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.8 and Gemini 3.1 Pro as judges
publication.summary: Adds a frozen-LLM preference model that ranks 15 unexecuted child solutions, optionally after short pilot runs, so AIRA-dojo executes only the most promising.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

At each child-creation step AIRA-dojo's draft, improve and debug operators produce 15 candidates; the RPM runs pairwise knockout comparisons with up to K previously executed nodes and their validation scores as context. The inference-only variant uses a MIPROv2-optimized prompt over plans and code; the agentic variant runs 5-minute pilot experiments in a cloned sandbox for draft and improve steps, sharing the agent's time budget. Only the chosen child is executed. Tasks: 20 text and tabular AIRS-Bench tasks, 10 seeds, 24 hours on one H200.
Results and comparison

Average normalized score rises from 0.684 (random choice among candidates) to 0.711 (inference-only) and 0.729 (agentic), against validation- and test-oracle ceilings of 0.748 and 0.759 that execute every candidate. Probability of improvement over the baseline is about 0.59 for both, with 95% intervals just above 0.5. The variants reach the baseline's 24-hour score in 14.88 and 15.50 hours. Reported task results are 94.1% on WinoGrande (v1 compares with 88.1%; v2 cites a 90.4% agentic SOTA) and 95.7% on SVAMP versus 94.2%.
Evaluation context

Offline development uses 1,000 sibling pairs from earlier greedy runs on 40 unreleased image, video and audio tasks, split by modality from the end-to-end tasks; single frontier-model judges (GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro) reach 64.66–67.44% pairwise accuracy versus 50% chance, and agentic pilots 78.52% at 5 minutes. Each end-to-end evaluation requires 200 H200 GPUs for 24 hours. Inference latency (0.660 h per run) is not charged; charging it gives 0.708. RPMs did not beat validation-based final-node selection. One scaffold, backbone and benchmark; no code release is named.

works.title: Ouroboros: A Self-Developing Frontier Coding Agent with Reviewed Core Evolution

publication.actor: Harness runs on Opus 5, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5 or GPT-5.6 Luna per benchmark; a multi-model LLM panel reviews self-commits
publication.summary: A deployed coding agent commits changes to its own tools, prompts and core code through a multi-model LLM review gate during a 161-day deployment.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A launcher and supervisor are separated from a mutable Git repository holding the task loop, tools, prompts, memory projection, review logic and benchmark adapters. Changes arrive through free evolution, where self-improvement is a task that can schedule the next cycle, or experience-driven evolution, where bugs exposed by work, reflection or user feedback become durable error classes and repairs. Every self-commit passes deterministic preflight, diff fingerprinting and a blocking multi-model review panel, optionally plus whole-repository scope review. Humans set runtime and review modes, hold an authenticated operator channel (task assignment, model routing, budget, /panic), and keep the constitution and spend cap outside agent control.
Results and comparison

Frozen benchmark seeds report Terminal-Bench 2.1 86.97% raw and 86.74% audited with Opus 5 (Claude Code with Fable 5: 83.8%), 84.3% with GPT-5.5 (Codex CLI 83.1%), OSWorld-Verified 90.69% (prior leader 90.19%), CL-Bench 0.2301 with Sonnet 4.6 (in-context learning 0.1960), SWE-bench Pro 58.2% versus Codex 59.4% after contamination filtering (p = 0.40), and GAIA 78.2% versus Claude Code 78.8%. The Hope deployment ran 161 days with 1,085 self-modification commits (94.2% agent-authored), 1,522 reviewed self-edit attempts, a recent review block rate of 63.5%, 79.7B tokens and $110.6K model spend.
Evaluation context

Benchmarks measure the harness at a frozen point, with no comparison against earlier seeds or a non-evolving control, so the contribution of self-development to the scores is not isolated. The deployment is a single lineage whose improvements are illustrated by case studies rather than a performance curve, and LLM reviewers can share the agent's blind spots. Trajectory audits removed one reward-hacked Terminal-Bench trial and filtered SWE-bench Pro instances where either agent reached the reference fix, which reversed the raw gap.

works.title: Mendel Godel Machine: Recursive Self-Improving Coding Agents via Comparative Evolution

publication.actor: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B performs self-modification and runs the coding agent; evolved scaffolds are also run on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro
publication.summary: Extends HGM-style archive search with self-edits conditioned on an agent's multi-task failure profile or on another lineage's trajectory for the same task.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

MGM keeps HGM's Thompson-sampling choice between evaluation and expansion but adds two expansion operators beside single-failure clonal mutation: reaction-norm mutation edits an agent from its trajectories on several tasks, and cross-lineage hybridization edits it using a reference agent's trajectory on a shared task, without copying code. A failed-task pool biases evaluation toward tasks other agents failed, raising overlap. Operator weights are fixed at 0.10/0.45/0.45. Self-modification and evaluation run in network-less containers. An additive fitness-landscape model and Monte Carlo simulation argue that comparative operators raise the chance an edit fixes a real defect.
Results and comparison

Under a matched budget of 200 evaluations and 24 expansions from the same ancestor, MGM reports 68.3%→78.3% on SWE-bench Verified-60 (HGM 73.3%) and 50.8%→93.2% on Polyglot-60 (HGM 77.9%), with similar wall-clock time on 8×H100 (96 vs 93 hours; 40 vs 44 hours). Removing reaction-norm mutation or hybridization lowers Polyglot-60 to 79.7% or 74.6%. Frozen, the Polyglot-evolved scaffold scores 26.7% on a 60-task SWE-bench Pro subset (initial 16.7%, HGM 13.3%) and 55.0% on SWE-bench Multilingual (41.7%, HGM 43.3%). The best agent solves 210 of 225 full Polyglot tasks (93.3%).
Evaluation context

Primary results come from fixed 60-task subsets under a single matched budget, and the same subsets drive final selection; the authors note limited seed diversity. HGM is the only real-run baseline, and DGM appears only in simulation. Moving the Verified-evolved scaffold to DeepSeek-V4-Pro gives 75.0% versus 45.0% for the initial scaffold and 70.0% for HGM's. A Qwen3-Coder-Next-80B-A3B backbone yields smaller gains (33.3%→41.7%). Appendix text quotes 61.7% for the Qwen3.6 Verified-60 result that Table 7 lists as 78.3%.

works.title: EurekAgent: Agent Environment Engineering is All You Need For Autonomous Scientific Discovery

publication.actor: Claude Code sessions running GLM-5.1 act as preparation, proposal and parallel implementation agents, with web-search and browser MCP tools. No model is trained.
publication.summary: Coordinates off-the-shelf CLI agents through propose–implement rounds in an engineered environment with hidden evaluators, isolation, Git artifacts, budgets and human-oversight interfaces.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Humans supply a problem description, a hidden evaluation script, a submission specification, optional initial code and budgets for time and API cost. One preparation session is followed by up to R rounds. Each round has a proposal session that may search the web and writes up to P hypotheses, then P parallel implementation sessions in isolated workspaces that cannot see each other within a round. The environment provides Docker isolation, a grading service that hides the evaluator, controller-owned result files, a GPU lock API, Git-tracked artifacts, a ranked solution history and chat-capable monitoring interfaces. Settings use R = 5–13, P = 3 and 100–160-minute implementation sessions.
Results and comparison

Circle packing reaches 2.635999 against 2.635986, the best previous AI result (R1-Distill-Qwen3-8B). Erdős' minimum overlap reaches 0.380870 and AC1 1.502861, against TTT-Discover's 0.380876 and 1.502863. The three mathematics runs average under $17 in API cost, and circle packing costs $11. On TriMul, regraded locally on an A100, the best kernel's median is 2005.03 µs, against 2096.04 µs for the top regraded human submission and 2247.78 µs for TTT-Discover's kernel. On a seven-competition MLE-Bench Lite subset, the any-medal rate is 85.71%, against 71.43% for each listed baseline.
Evaluation context

Each task is a single run, and the paper reports no ablation that removes individual environment dimensions. The mathematics margins are in the sixth decimal place. In circle packing, round 2 found and adopted the public AlphaEvolve solution through web search before improving on it. TriMul was evaluated locally because the leaderboard had closed. The MLE-Bench subset was sampled by difficulty tier from public leaderboard medal rates. Baselines are quoted at the upper end of their reported ranges and use closed models. The paper does not say whether humans intervened during the reported runs.

works.title: MLEvolve: A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery

publication.actor: All agents (planner, coder, code review, data leakage, fusion and others): Gemini-3.1-Pro-preview; other backbones tried on a task subset
publication.summary: Searches over full ML pipelines with Monte Carlo graph search, cross-branch reference edges, within-task retrieval memory, and a planner-coder split with diff edits.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each node is a complete pipeline (preprocessing, features, training, prediction). Progressive MCGS decays UCT exploration and softly switches to elite-guided exploitation; stagnation triggers intra-branch evolution, cross-branch reference or multi-branch aggregation. Node rewards are −1, 1 or 2 for failure, valid non-improvement and branch improvement. Retrospective memory pairs a curated domain knowledge base for cold start with a per-task record of plans, outcomes and errors retrieved by BM25 plus FAISS. Budget per task: 12 hours, 500 steps, one H200, three parallel branches.
Results and comparison

On all 75 MLE-bench tasks (mean of 3 seeds) MLEvolve reports a 65.3% medal rate and 34.7% gold rate in 12 hours, versus 63.1% for AIBuildAI (Claude-Opus-4.6, 24 h), 62.7% for MARS+ (Gemini-3-Pro-preview, 24 h) and 31.6% for AIRA-dojo (o3, 24 h). In MLE-bench Lite ablations, removing Progressive MCGS or memory lowers the medal rate from 81.82% to 68.18%, and one-shot coding gives 72.73%. On 15 AlphaEvolve math problems it reports the best value on 11.
Evaluation context

Baseline numbers are copied from the leaderboard or the original papers and use different LLMs and time budgets, so the comparison mixes model and harness effects. Main results use 3 seeds; component ablations use the 22-task Lite set and finer mechanism analyses a 9-task subset. Self-evolution here means memory and search adaptation within a single task run; agent code and model weights stay fixed. Token and dollar costs are not reported.

works.title: MUSE-Autoskill: Self-Evolving Agents via Skill Creation, Memory, Management, and Evaluation

publication.actor: GPT-5.5 (gpt-5.5-2026-04-24) backs MUSE-Autoskill and the Codex, Claude Code and Hermes comparison agents
publication.summary: An agent creates skill packages from its own successful trajectories, tests them in a sandbox, stores per-skill notes and refines failing skills.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A ReAct agent with a built-in skill_create tool writes SKILL.md packages, optionally with scripts and pytest tests, blocks registration until sandbox tests or runtime checks pass, and patches failing skills. Each skill carries an append-only .memory.md of usage notes alongside short- and long-term memory, and context is a turn DAG with two-level compression above 180K tokens. On SkillsBench, Phase 1 solves each task without skills; Phase 2 re-runs the task five times with a skill distilled from a successful Phase 1 trajectory.
Results and comparison

On the 75-task SkillsBench common set, MUSE-Autoskill scores 46.95% without skills, 53.42% with self-created skills and 59.67% with human-written skills; Codex and Claude Code reach 47.52% and 44.27% with their own skills. On the 47 covered tasks, self-created skills reach 85.24% versus 81.17% with human skills, at 499K versus 638K median tokens. MUSE-created skills raise Hermes from 37.24% to 51.90%, while Codex-created skills give 37.01%. Turning memory on lifts a SkillLearnBench feedback round from 60% to 74%.
Evaluation context

Each self-created skill is distilled from one successful trajectory and re-evaluated on the same task, which the authors note may overstate gains; 28 of 75 tasks yield no usable skill and count as zero. Transfer is tested only into Hermes, and the largest self-created regression, hvac-control, falls from 80% to 20%. SkillLearnBench (100 instances, one run each) gives 43.0%→48.0% with self-created skills versus 72.0% with human skills. Production adoption at ByteDance is described without measurements.

works.title: Effective Harness Engineering for Algorithm Discovery with Coding Agents

publication.actor: Codex-CLI coding agents on gpt-5.2-codex or gpt-5.1-codex-mini write candidates; a separate gpt-5.1-codex-mini agent flags evaluation hacks; the OpenEvolve baseline calls the same models statelessly.
publication.summary: Replaces stateless LLM mutation calls with multi-step coding agents in isolated git worktrees, adding an agent-based evaluation-hack filter to island-model evolution.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Each candidate is a git branch; up to four agents work in parallel worktrees, run the evaluator, debug within one session and can optionally query an SQLite database of past attempts. Island-model settings (5 islands, migration every 50 algorithms) follow OpenEvolve defaults for both systems, and runs stop at a 40M-token ceiling. Humans supply the Circle Packing (n=26) task, evaluator and seed; candidates flagged as hacks are excluded from parent selection.
Results and comparison

Best of two runs: Vesper with gpt-5.2-codex reaches 2.63599 versus 2.54142 for OpenEvolve with the same model and 2.41852 for OpenEvolve with gpt-5.2 (AlphaEvolve 2.6358, human 2.6340), using 89.6K tokens per algorithm for 452 algorithms versus 23.9K for 1,671. With OpenEvolve's budget raised to 146M tokens (about $392, Vesper's estimated spend) it plateaus at 2.502. The hack filter excluded 7.8% of gpt-5.2-codex algorithms (16.6% with database access) and none from gpt-5.1-codex-mini; database access did not improve scores.
Evaluation context

One task and two runs per condition; the reported 'Best' is the maximum over runs, so no variance is given. Conditions without the hack filter reached raw scores above 10 and were reported only after mechanically discarding scores above 3. Dollar figures use blended billing rates. The comparison swaps the whole harness at once, so the gain is not attributed to a single component; worktree isolation gave 3.2–3.9× wall-clock speedups with four agents.

works.title: SkillOS: Learning Skill Curation for Self-Evolving Agents

publication.actor: Qwen3-8B skill curator trained with GRPO; frozen executors Qwen3-8B (training), Qwen3-32B, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite; Qwen3-32B scores skill content
publication.summary: Trains a skill curator with RL to insert, update and delete Markdown skills that a frozen executor retrieves on later related tasks.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

A Qwen3-8B curator is trained with GRPO on grouped streams of related tasks: the repository starts empty, the frozen executor retrieves skills with BM25, and the curator edits the repository after each task. The reward combines success on later tasks in the group, valid function calls, a Qwen3-32B content-quality score and a conciseness term. Gemini-2.5-Pro annotates task attributes for grouping, and reasoning training uses a 33,000-problem DeepMath-103k subset. Training runs on 16 H100s for about 3 days (ALFWorld), 5 days (WebShop) and 2.5 days (reasoning).
Results and comparison

With a Qwen3-8B executor, ALFWorld success rises from 47.9 (no memory) and 55.7 (ReasoningBank) to 61.2, WebShop success from 9.8 to 16.5, and the AIME24/AIME25/GPQA-Diamond average from 69.6 to 73.8. The same curator lifts a Gemini-2.5-Pro executor on ALFWorld from 66.4 to 80.2. The RL-trained 8B curator beats Gemini-2.5-Pro used as an untrained curator (61.2 vs 50.7 with the Qwen3-8B executor). Training on random task orders instead of grouped streams lowers ALFWorld success to 57.3.
Evaluation context

Results average three runs on benchmark test sets after training on the training splits. Executor transfer holds the trained curator fixed; cross-domain transfer is mostly positive but includes cells from −0.7 to −2.8 points. The correctness signal given to the curator comes from an LLM judge using the frozen executor. Skills are single Markdown files without scripts. Curator inference cost per task is not reported separately, although ALFWorld episodes shorten by 2.2–3.1 steps and fewer skills are used per example.

works.title: SkillClaw: Let Skills Evolve Collectively with Agentic Evolver

publication.actor: Qwen3-Max runs the OpenClaw agents, the agentic evolver and the validation comparison
publication.summary: Aggregates multi-user agent sessions by skill and lets an LLM evolver refine or create shared skills, deploying only validated updates.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Deployed OpenClaw agents record sessions with prompts, tool calls, errors and outcomes; sessions are grouped by the skills they invoked and passed to an LLM evolver that chooses refine, create or skip. At night, each candidate and the current skill are re-run on relevant tasks collected that day in idle user environments, and the model compares outcomes on task success and execution stability. Only accepted updates are synchronized to all users. The experiment simulates 8 concurrent users over 6 day–night rounds on WildClawBench.
Results and comparison

Reported Day 1→Day 6 scores are 54.01%→60.34% for Social Interaction, 22.73%→34.55% for Search & Retrieval, 11.57%→21.80% for Creative Synthesis and 24.00%→32.00% for Safety & Alignment. Most gains come from updates accepted after the first night; many later candidates were rejected, and Creative Synthesis kept only its Night 1 update. A controlled test on three custom queries reports an average of 30.4%→72.5% after one evolution round, with the smallest gain on deadline parsing (41.1%→48.0%).
Evaluation context

This is a small simulated deployment. Four of six WildClawBench categories are reported, and validation and reported scores draw on the same benchmark task pool rather than a held-out split. The validator is the same Qwen3-Max model that executes and evolves skills. No other skill-evolution method is compared, repeated runs are not reported, and the extra token cost of nightly validation is acknowledged but not quantified.

works.title: POLARIS: A Godel Agent Framework for Small Language Models through Experience-Abstracted Policy Repair

publication.actor: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct both repairs and runs its own policy; further runs use Qwen3-8B and devstral-small-2 (24B, 4-bit)
publication.summary: A 7B-model Godel-style agent turns batches of validation failures into abstracted strategies and minimal code patches to its own policy.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Built on the Godel Agent code, each repair cycle runs the current policy on a validation set, takes N = 3 or 5 failed instances, and has the model write a diagnosis, revision and prevention record per failure, synthesize one or two reusable strategy directives, and emit minimal code patches. Patches are accepted after syntax and execution checks with up to three retries, not after a score check; reflections, strategies and failed patches stay in memory, and tool-call history is cut from ten to six messages to fit small-model context. Runs evolve for 10 hours on two V100 GPUs; humans supply the adapted goal prompt and repair templates.
Results and comparison

Direct replication of Godel Agent with Qwen2.5-7B failed: with five prior tool-call messages, 18 of 20 runs were unsuccessful and none improved; with three, one DROP run improved. Across ten Qwen2.5-7B POLARIS runs per dataset at N = 3, 5 (MGSM), 3 (DROP), 4 (GPQA) and 6 (LitBench) improved test performance, while 4, 5, 2 and 3 runs failed through out-of-memory errors, loops or hallucinated tool calls. The best successful runs exceed CoT-SC by +4.0% (MGSM), +3.9% (DROP), +9.0% (GPQA) and +8.8% (LitBench).
Evaluation context

Headline gains are maxima over successful runs rather than means, test sets are small (250 questions for MGSM, DROP and LitBench; 100 for GPQA), and patch acceptance does not check validation score, so trajectories are non-monotonic. Qwen3-8B gave 4, 2, 3 and 4 successful runs out of five at N = 3, and devstral-small-2 had 3 unsuccessful runs out of 20, suggesting many failures are resource-bound. DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B consistently failed. The repair operators themselves stay fixed.

works.title: EvoX: Meta-Evolution for Automated Discovery

publication.actor: GPT-5 or Gemini-3.0-Pro generates candidate solutions; GPT-5 writes the search-strategy code; a lightweight model instantiates operator prompts; task evaluators are fixed.
publication.summary: Co-evolves candidate programs and the search strategy that selects parents, inspirations and variation operators, rewriting the strategy when progress stalls.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

An inner loop evolves solutions for a window of W iterations (10% of the budget) under the current strategy. If best-score improvement in the window falls below a threshold, GPT-5 writes a new strategy conditioned on a population-state descriptor and a database of earlier strategies scored by windowed progress; the solution population is kept across switches. Strategies choose parents, inspiration sets and one of three operators (local refinement, structural variation, free-form). Every run starts from uniform random parent sampling. Humans supply the task, evaluator and seed program.
Results and comparison

With 100 iterations for every open framework and three runs per cell, EvoX reports the best mean on 6 of 8 math tasks with GPT-5 and 7 of 8 with Gemini-3.0-Pro, and the best mean on all 6 ADRS systems tasks with GPT-5 (5 of 6 with Gemini). On 172 Frontier-CS problems (GPT-5) it reports mean 62.6 / median 75.5 versus 50.5 / 56.2 for OpenEvolve; on 10 ALE-Bench-Lite tasks an average private score of 1958.2 versus 1914.6 for a ShinkaEvolve reproduction. AlphaEvolve values are copied from its paper, whose budget is unknown.
Evaluation context

Budgets match solution evaluations, not tokens or dollars, so strategy-generation calls are additional; only a Heilbronn-triangle cost plot reports dollars (EvoX and GEPA under $1 to pass 0.031, versus $7.6 for ShinkaEvolve and $15.4 for OpenEvolve). Three runs per cell; several margins sit in the fourth decimal, and headline system wins such as PRISM 30.52 are best-of-three (mean 27.67). Some appendix cells, e.g. the GPT-5 signal-processing mean, differ from the main tables. Frontier-CS and ALE-Bench use GPT-5 only.

works.title: Huxley-Godel Machine: Human-Level Coding Agent Development by an Approximation of the Optimal Self-Improving Machine

publication.actor: Self-modification by GPT-5 (SWE-bench) or quantized Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B (Polyglot); evaluation by GPT-5-mini or Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B
publication.summary: Coding agents edit their own code in a tree search that expands nodes by clade-level descendant success rather than each agent's own benchmark score.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Self-improvement is cast as tree search with separate expand and evaluate actions. Clade-metaproductivity (CMP) is estimated from pooled successes and failures of an agent's descendants; Thompson sampling picks parents to expand and agents to evaluate one task at a time, and a UCB-Air rule decides when to expand. Execution is asynchronous across CPUs. The initial agent comes from the DGM code (bash and file-edit tools), and the returned agent is the best-belief node under a beta posterior. A theorem shows that a true CMP oracle suffices to reproduce Godel-machine acceptance under stated assumptions.
Results and comparison

With 800 task evaluations from the same ancestor, HGM reports 56.7% on SWE-bench Verified-60 (from 40%) in 517 allocated CPU-hours, versus DGM 53.3% in 1,231 hours and SICA 50.0% (stalled on context-length errors after 360 evaluations). On Polyglot it reports 30.5% (from 20.3%) in 347 hours, versus DGM 27.1% (2,385 hours) and SICA 25.4% (572 hours). HGM's CMP estimate correlates 0.778 and 0.626 (weighted) with empirical clade outcomes, versus 0.285 and 0.383 for DGM's selection metric. An 8,000-evaluation run on full SWE-bench Verified with GPT-5-mini moves a 53.2% ancestor to 61.4%.
Evaluation context

Verified-60 and full-Verified scores are measured on the tasks used for search. On SWE-bench Lite with the 93 Verified-overlapping tasks removed, the evolved agent scores 40.1% versus 34.8% for its ancestor and 39.6% for SWE-agent with GPT-5-mini; with GPT-5 swapped in it scores 47.8% versus 48.3% for the leaderboard SWE-agent (Claude 4 Sonnet). The search policy (CMP estimator, sampling rules) is fixed and human-designed; only agent code self-modifies. No repeated-seed variance is reported, and total spend is about $5,000 across all methods.

works.title: CodeEvolve: An open source evolutionary coding agent for algorithm discovery and optimization

publication.actor: v1: Gemini 2.5 Flash (80%) and Pro (20%) propose diff edits, with Flash as the meta-prompting model; v6 adds Qwen3-Coder-30B and four other backbones. Evaluators are fixed.
publication.summary: Evolves programs and their prompts across islands with rank-based depth refinement, inspiration-based crossover, meta-prompted exploration and, in later versions, CVT-MAP-Elites archives.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Five islands in v1 (ten in v6 comparisons) hold solution and prompt populations with ring migration. Exploitation samples a parent by rank and shows its ancestors; exploration has an auxiliary LLM rewrite the parent's prompt before generation; inspiration solutions in context act as multi-parent crossover. Candidates run in sandboxes with time and memory limits, and failures score zero. Humans supply the problem prompt, a trivial seed program and the evaluator. v6 adds a plateau-triggered exploration scheduler and per-island CVT-MAP-Elites.
Results and comparison

v1 (Gemini 2.5, one reported best per problem) claims to beat AlphaEvolve on five of six instances, including circle packing n=26 (2.63596 vs 2.63586) and the second autocorrelation inequality (0.93768 vs 0.89627). v6 lists the latter as 0.88110 (Qwen3-Coder-30B) against an AlphaEvolve value of 0.96102 and reports matching or surpassing AlphaEvolve on 5 of 9 instances. In v6's controlled comparison (Qwen3-Coder-30B, three runs, matched evaluation budgets) it has the best mean on 6 of 9 problems, e.g. circle packing n=26 mean 2.63576 vs 2.54962 (OpenEvolve) and 2.47568 (ShinkaEvolve).
Evaluation context

AlphaEvolve and ThetaEvolve comparisons use reported numbers with unmatched budgets. v1 reports one best run per problem without seeds, and LLM API nondeterminism prevents exact replication. v6 adds three-run means, ablations and cost: on circle packing n=26, Qwen3-Coder-30B passed AlphaEvolve's score after about 900 calls (about $6) versus about 400 calls (about $35) for Gemini 2.5. EoH comparisons reuse EoH's GPT-3.5-turbo results with matched call counts. Headline values change across six arXiv versions.

works.title: Scientific Algorithm Discovery by Augmenting AlphaEvolve with Deep Research

publication.actor: Fixed OpenAI models by role: o4-mini plans and reflects, gpt-4o searches the web, o3-mini writes proposals and code, and o4-mini debugs. The evolved programs train task-specific models on one GPU.
publication.summary: Adds web-grounded research proposals, cross-file code edits and a debugging agent to an AlphaEvolve-style island and MAP-Elites program database.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

In each iteration, a planner writes 5–10 research questions and a searcher summarizes web results. A writer proposes 3–10 ideas with pseudo-code and self-scores for originality, potential and difficulty. A coder applies diffs across files, and a debugger gets up to five attempts. Candidates come from up to 25 programs on five islands, with MAP-Elites inspirations. Humans supply the problem description, evaluation code and data, an initial algorithm (GREA, OpenEvolve's SLSQP packer, CodePDE or Kaggle participant baselines) and instructions with a 30-minute, one-GPU (2080 Ti or A6000) runtime limit. Runs allow 50–200 iterations.
Results and comparison

Across nine tasks, scores improve over the initial algorithms by 0.39% (Open Vaccine, 0.7187→0.7214) to 666.02% (circle packing averaged over 26–32 circles, 0.3891→2.9806, where the initial packer often produced invalid packings). Molecular Translation rises from 0.1885 to 0.2562, Polymer Prediction from 0.6770 to 0.7714 and Molecular Prediction from 0.7915 to 0.8149. Without deep research, where evolution relies only on the models' internal knowledge, the best molecule score is 0.797 against 0.815, and circle packing 2.735 against 2.981. Debugging raises execution success on Open Vaccine from 0.130 to 0.990.
Evaluation context

The baselines are the initial algorithms and a two-task ablation without deep research, not budget-matched external systems. Each task reports one score with no variance, and the reported score is the one used to pick the best version. The appendix notes that some components described in evolved versions were placeholders or never ran (a soft edit-distance loss, an IMEX-Euler path, wavelet preprocessing). Originality is judged by an LLM, and API cost is not reported. Seven tasks are model-training pipelines for scientific prediction.

works.title: DeepScientist: Advancing Frontier-Pushing Scientific Findings Progressively

publication.actor: Core logic, hypotheses and LLM surrogate reviewer: Gemini-2.5-Pro; implementation: Claude-4-Opus in Claude Code; three human experts verify outputs
publication.summary: Runs month-long Bayesian-optimization-style research loops that rank ideas with an LLM surrogate, implement the top pick on a SOTA codebase, and log findings to memory.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Humans choose three tasks and manually reproduce a published baseline for each: All at Once on Who&When, Token Recycling on MBPP, and Fast-DetectGPT on RAID (compared against Binoculars). A Findings Memory stores papers, code and every prior idea and result; an LLM surrogate scores new ideas for utility, quality and exploration, a UCB rule picks one to implement in a sandboxed copy of the baseline repository, and ideas that beat the baseline receive extra analyses and an auto-written paper. Runs used 16 H800 GPUs, one instance per GPU.
Results and comparison

Reported gains over the human starting points: Who&When accuracy 12.07%→29.31% (hand-crafted) and 16.67%→47.46% (algorithm-generated); MBPP decoding throughput 190.25→193.90 tokens/s; RAID AUROC 0.800→0.863 with latency 117→60 ms. About 5,000 ideas led to about 1,100 implementations and 21 progress findings. Randomly sampled ideas reportedly give near-zero success versus 1–3% with selection, and a one-week scaling run found 1 finding with 4 GPUs versus 11 with 16.
Evaluation context

Results come from one month-long exploration with no repeated runs, each measured against a single chosen baseline. Three human experts supervised throughout to verify outputs and filter hallucinations, and all results were manually inspected. In a sample of failed trials about 60% ended in implementation errors. A three-person committee rated the five generated papers 5.00 on average (ICLR 2025 average 5.08), citing weak validation and missing baselines. Total cost was about $100,000 and over 20,000 GPU hours.

works.title: AI Research Agents for Machine Learning: Search, Exploration, and Generalization in MLE-bench

publication.scope: Search policies and operators for MLE agents
publication.actor: Operators: DeepSeek R1 (20 seeds per task) or o3 (10 seeds per task); GPT-4o parses execution output; o1-preview for one AIDE baseline
publication.summary: Recasts ML research agents as graph search over code, varying operators and greedy, MCTS or evolutionary policies on MLE-bench lite in a sandboxed dojo.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Agents run in Apptainer containers with one H200, 24 CPU cores, 100 GB RAM, a 24-hour limit and 4 hours per execution. Each node is a full solution script scored by 5-fold cross-validation. The AIRA operator set adds prompt-adaptive complexity, scoped memory (siblings for draft and improve, ancestors for debug), explicit thinking and a crossover operator to AIDE's draft, debug and improve operators. Search policies are greedy, MCTS (UCT, no rollouts) and fitness-proportional evolution, evaluated on the 22-task MLE-bench lite.
Results and comparison

With AIDE's operators, MCTS and evolutionary search give no gain over greedy (34.6–39.8% medal rate with R1). With AIRA operators and R1, greedy rises from 39.8% to 45.5% and MCTS reaches 47.1%; the headline 39.6%→47.7% corresponds to AIDE greedy and AIRA greedy with o3. Running AIDE greedy with o1-preview inside the dojo lifts the 35.2% reported by MLE-bench to 45.9%. Choosing the final node by test rather than validation score would add 9–13 points.
Evaluation context

Results use 20 seeds per task with R1 and 10 with o3 on 22 tasks; the authors show agent rankings can flip with 3–5 seeds and recommend at least 10. Validation-guided search overfits: agent-perceived medal rates keep rising while test performance plateaus, and in runs extended to 90–120 hours AIRA MCTS deteriorates after about 50 hours. The paper flags possible contamination of Kaggle tasks in LLM training data. A later version adds full 75-task results (31.6% for AIRA greedy with o3).

works.title: The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search

publication.actor: Code generation: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (v2); LLM/VLM feedback and summary agents: GPT-4o; write-up reflection uses reasoning models such as o1
publication.summary: Replaces v1's code templates with a four-stage, experiment-manager-guided agentic tree search over experiment code, then writes and VLM-reviews a workshop paper.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Humans supply a broad topic prompt; idea generation queries Semantic Scholar for novelty. An experiment manager runs four stages (prototype, hyperparameter tuning, research agenda, ablations) with node budgets of 21, 12, 12 and 12, a one-hour cap per node and debug depth 3. Buggy nodes are debugged and working nodes refined; an LLM evaluator picks the best node per stage, replicated runs supply means and standard deviations, and a VLM critiques figures. One paper takes several hours, up to a 15-hour limit.
Results and comparison

Three manuscripts were submitted blind to the ICLR 2025 ICBINB workshop, which received 43 submissions. One, a negative-result study of a compositional regularizer on synthetic arithmetic data, received scores 6, 7 and 6 (mean 6.33, roughly top 45%) and would have been accepted; the other two were rejected. By prior agreement with the organizers and under UBC IRB approval, the accepted paper was withdrawn after review.
Evaluation context

Humans chose the workshop theme, picked three of roughly 40 generated ideas, ran each with several seeds and selected the best manuscript per idea by inspection, so the outcome is a best-of-selection result rather than a success rate. The authors' internal review judged none of the papers main-conference quality and found inaccurate citations, an unclear description of what is regularized, possible dataset overlap and inaccurate figure captions. Dollar cost is not reported.

works.title: Godel Agent: A Self-Referential Agent Framework for Recursive Self-Improvement

publication.actor: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) runs the self-improving agent; optimized policies and baselines are scored with gpt-3.5-turbo-0125
publication.summary: An LLM agent reads and monkey-patches its own runtime code, rewriting both its task policy and the routine it uses to improve itself.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Starting from a Chain-of-Thought policy and a task-agnostic goal prompt, the agent recursively chooses actions: inspect its own code in Python runtime memory, score the current policy on a validation set, patch the policy or its own improvement logic via monkey patching, or recurse. Humans supply the benchmark interface and utility function, an error-handling wrapper, a 'thinking before acting' step, and code-execution and LLM-calling tools. Each benchmark gets six independent cycles of up to 30 iterations on 128 validation questions (32 for GPQA); the optimized policy is then scored on 800 test questions (166 for GPQA).
Results and comparison

In the constrained Godel-base setting (policies call gpt-3.5-turbo), reported test scores are DROP F1 80.9, MGSM 64.2%, MMLU 70.9% and GPQA 34.9%, versus 79.4, 53.4%, 69.6% and 34.6% for Meta Agent Search; baseline numbers are copied from the ADAS paper. The unconstrained Godel-free variant reaches 90.5, 90.6%, 87.9% and 55.7%, mainly because evolved policies call stronger models such as GPT-4o, so it is not a like-for-like comparison. On MGSM, removing thinking or error handling lowers accuracy to 50.8% and 49.4%. A full 30-step run over the four datasets costs about $15, against the $300 the authors cite for Meta Agent Search.
Evaluation context

Edits to the improvement routine itself are shown through case studies (on Game of 24 the agent switched to exhaustive search and reached 100%, and added error-trace analysis and parallel optimization) rather than measured separately from policy gains. In 100 MGSM trials, 92% showed temporary drops, 4% terminated unexpectedly (typically after the agent edited its own recursion module), and 14% ended below the initial policy. Runs started from weaker policies never surpassed a Tree-of-Thought start. Validation sets are small, and numbers here are from the v4 revision.

works.title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems

publication.actor: GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) meta agent designs agents; discovered agents and baselines run on gpt-3.5-turbo-0125
publication.summary: A fixed GPT-4o meta agent programs new agents as Python forward functions, conditioning on a growing archive of evaluated designs.
details: Method and supplied infrastructure

Agents are Python forward() functions inside a framework of under 100 lines that wraps foundation-model calls. Each iteration, the meta agent (Meta Agent Search) reads the archive, seeded with hand-designed agents such as CoT, CoT-SC, Self-Refine and LLM Debate, proposes an idea and its code, self-reflects twice for novelty and bugs, debugs up to five times on runtime errors, and adds the evaluated agent to the archive. Search runs 25 iterations on ARC (20 validation, 60 test questions) and 30 iterations per reasoning domain (128 validation, 800 test; GPQA 32/166). Humans supply domain descriptions, the framework and evaluators.
Results and comparison

With gpt-3.5-turbo running agents, reported held-out scores are DROP F1 79.4 (best hand-designed Role Assignment 65.8; OPRO prompt optimization 69.1), MGSM 53.4% (LLM Debate 39.0%), MMLU 69.6% (OPRO 67.6%) and GPQA 34.6% (OPRO 32.9%). The top MGSM agent transfers to GSM8K at 69.5% versus 43.6% for LLM Debate and to GSM-Hard at 31.2% versus 18.0% for Role Assignment.
